en: *Collection of the Elite of the Tiantai School*, Volume Two.
Recorded by Pūrṇa, Disciple of Xian-du.
Correct Meaning of the Śrāvakas, Three Records on the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, Record on the Vaipulya [Sūtras], and Differences in the Assembly of the Manifested Body.
The Dragon Girl Attaining Buddhahood: Esoteric Teachings; Indeterminate Teachings; The Designation of *T'i-wei* as Belonging to the Three Doubts;
Expedient and Real; Ānanda Begging for Milk:
The Orthodox Meaning of the Śrāvakas.

When the Sage appears in the world, he universally establishes the teachings of the five periods for the various capacities within the Dharma-realm; yet these primarily reach the assembly of those of the Two Vehicles.

This is because they had previously received the seeds of the Great Vehicle from the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, which he held within his breast. However, having temporarily regressed from Great Bodhi, they have long wandered through the cycle of birth and death across the five destinies.
Out of compassion, the Tathāgata arises in response to appear among them; first, he employs the four preceding periods as skillful means to guide and prepare them.

Next, regarding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, its convergence toward the Buddha-way through the three turnings of the wheel reveals the distinction between those with sharp and dull faculties who receive their predictions;

the four types of śrāvakas differ in whether their names are expanded or condensed. The meanings of the sūtra and its commentaries are vast, and the terminology of the sub-commentaries (*śāstra*) and records is so abundant that those of shallow learning cannot fathom their source, nor can those of inferior intelligence exhaust their purport.
Consequently, in the course of my lectures, I have examined various texts to establish the fundamental principles.

There is a definitive determination of the nature [of the teachings] that leads to their ultimate destination; this treatise on the great elements (*mahābhūta*) relies upon the sutras and follows the commentaries, and I do not dare to speak from mere conjecture.
Should there be any points that differ from ancient or modern views, I shall set forth my humble opinions in four parts: first, distinguishing between the secondary and primary root-natures;

second, investigating the existence or non-existence of the great elements; third, clarifying the eight gates of the *pitaka* and *āgama*; and fourth, indicating the purport of the text and resolving doubts and obstacles.
First, regarding the analysis of the derivative and primary capacities of the faculties, the text states:

"The provisional city" (the *parīttābha* or *śrāvaka* stage) has as its primary intent the withdrawal of those of great capacity who would otherwise take up the path of the small, while it serves as a derivative means for those of small capacity to set out in their training. Regarding the first two weeks, the primary intent is for those of small capacity to set out in their training, while the derivative intent is for those of great capacity to withdraw.
For now, the derivative aspect concerning the withdrawal of those of great capacity is set aside and not discussed; the primary intent is for them to set out in their training.
Regarding how to categorize those who study the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) within the four types of people:

if they are of fixed nature and do not reach the stage of the *Lotus Sūtra*’s "arrogance," they are briefly categorized as those who "clear their seats and depart. This is because they represent the provisional practice of transformation. Therefore, they are not discussed [in this context]. It is asked:

"If one retreats from the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) while remaining attached to the provisional, neither advancing nor retreating will be achieved; how then should this be judged? Some say: "Setting out by studying the Lesser Vehicle is appropriate [for such a case]."
That which is subsumed under the "response-body transformation" (nirmāṇakāya) is revealed through three cycles and does not exceed the two types of śrāvakas who regress from the Great Vehicle.
As the treatise states: "The first two have not yet matured and are not given the prediction; the latter two are given the prediction. This is precisely what is meant.

Some say that those subsumed under "regression from the Great Vehicle" refer to the two types of root-natures—those who wait for the time and those who do not wait—and that the first two cycles pertain to those who wait for the time.

For this reason, it is called "Setting Out" (*fa-zhen*). Because those who study the Small [Vehicle] do not wait for their time, it is said that they "retreat by way of the peripheral" (*bangwei tui da*).

Some say that "the first two cycles are peripheral retreats from the Great" refers to the third stage; although their innate capacities (*xinggen*) have encountered the Dharma through parables, they have not yet attained realization.
They merely destroy the ignorance (*avidyā*) of the *Pǐnpǐn* (Shorter Version) and have not yet entered the initial stage of the Perfect Family (*yuánjiā*).

Regarding "staying by the side": because they remain in their seats, it is said that for those who have regressed from the Great Vehicle, they stay by the side. Regarding "setting out by the side" for those who study the Lesser Vehicle:
these individuals had already attained awakening and entry into the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) of the Perfect Teaching during the two cycles of the Dharma and the Parable;

thus, when they heard the matters of Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū during the cycle of the Causes and Conditions—concerning the increase of the Path and the diminution of births—they were able to remain in their seats without hindrance. Therefore, it is said that for those studying the Lesser Vehicle, they set out by the side.

However, the intended meaning of these three explanations is not as the first master asserts— that the initial departure was originally small and the judgment belongs to the provisional transformation,

thereby revealing that this present sutra’s revelation is specifically for those of gradual practice; nor as the second master asserts— that if one distinguishes between the peripheral and the primary based on whether they await the time or do not await it,
then the two previous weeks were primarily for those who had begun their training as small-capacity individuals, while the parable of the hearing of the Dharma refers to the present.

To claim that [the teaching] was "incidentally" for the sake of those who had regressed from the Great Vehicle upon hearing the *nidāna*, or "specifically" for the sake of those who had regressed from the Great Vehicle upon hearing the *parīttābha* (the "burning city"), might be acceptable.

However, as for the claim that it was "incidentally" for the sake of those who had set out to study the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), I do not yet understand what Dharma they heard or what benefit they obtained.
This single question alone reveals the error of the third master’s theory; while it may seem plausible at first glance, further investigation shows it to be incorrect.

Furthermore, it is asked: since the two preceding cycles (the *nidāna* and the *parivarta*) are peripheral, and people of that time merely destroyed the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra in Eight Thousand Lines* without yet attaining awakening or entry [into the truth], it would not be improper for those present at the assembly to have been of dull faculties.
Why then did Jingxi say that those who "receded from the Great" were of sharp faculties throughout the two preceding cycles?
Since the departure [from the Lesser] in the *nidāna* cycle was already set in motion within the two preceding cycles, they must have attained awakening and entry therein.
From the first *yuanzhù* (stage of perfecting) up to the completion of the causal conditions, the path increases and birth is diminished; this should pertain to those of sharp faculties.

Why then does Jingxi say that those who were originally of the Small Vehicle are dull-witted and should belong to the third [category]? Upon encountering this question, one ought to remain speechless.

Furthermore, there are those who attempt to resolve the texts concerning the "auxiliary" and "primary" by applying the nine cycles of the general and specific [teachings]; such groundless talk is not worth evaluating. This is my current view.
One should know that bringing [the teaching] forth so as to eliminate doubt and stagnation involves initiating the study of the *Hīnayāna* to discuss the fourfold classification of the *Madhyamaka*.

This is precisely what is subsumed under the "receding from the Great" (*mahāyāna*). These are attached to the three cycles (*triparivarta*), which differ in their names; thus, the distinction between the secondary and the primary is divided.

If it concerns the first two cycles, because the faculties are sharp, there is no need to point back to the past; one is able to believe and understand immediately, and therefore it is called "initiation" (*pravṛtti*).

The *Zhēn* [commentary] states that because his study of the Small Vehicle was slight and his faculties were dull, he had to rely on being shown the past events of Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū before he could attain realization;
therefore, it is said that he "retreated from the Great. As the *Miaole* says: "When explaining by means of the Dharma, we do not yet discuss the remote past, but rather rely on the present text.
Here, "the name 'setting out to study the Small' is based on the present text. The *Wénjù* says: "The City of Transformation is precisely..."
Regarding the statement in the *Wuwei Taide Miaole* (The Sublime Joy of Withdrawing from the Great [Vehicle], etc.

that "the primary intent of the 'transformed city' is for the purpose of withdrawing from the Great [Vehicle]," this is further discussed in comparison with the similarities and differences of the two preceding weeks. Therefore, the present text states: "The path ahead is still long; now we wish to turn back.
In the two preceding weeks, these words did not yet exist; it was only said that they were submerged in suffering and burned. This is also a general interpretation, and it may be so.

Those who "retreated from the Great" were those with sharp faculties who had previously attained [the path] during the first two weeks; those who were originally "Small" were those of dull faculties who should have been in the third week. Regarding what is said about their similarities and differences:
they are the same in that they all received predictions (vyākaraṇa) during the three weeks, as they were all people who had retreated from the Great Vehicle. Thus, the *Shiqian* states:

"The assembly that received predictions during the two weeks of the Dharma and the Parable were none other than those who had established karmic connections in the past. They differ, however, in that during the two weeks of the Dharma and the Parable...
The *Zhōu* (the *Fahua xuanyi*) refers to this as "starting the carriage," while the *Xue* (the *Fahua wenju*) speaks of "retreating from the Great" due to small causes and conditions.

Because of the sharpness or dullness of their faculties, two names are established to clarify their similarities and differences. The ancestral intent is clear and cool, yet students remain ignorant of it;

not understanding this, how can they definitively judge the three "weeks" (*zhōu*) of revelation and the specific capacities of the beings they address? Now, I shall point this out for you so that the truth may be revealed.

Justice allows for no excess; thus, although the three cycles involve retreating from the Great [Vehicle] to the Small, whether categorized as lateral or primary, none of them deviate from those who have retreated from the Great.
If Tiantai refers to this as "setting out by studying the Small," it is a name established through metaphorical illustration;

if Jingxi refers to it as "originally dwelling in the Small," it is a designation received according to the Dharma. Although these names differ based on the capacities of those benefited—whether sharp or dull—the underlying principle remains the same.

If it is merely this single "one," then since you claim that the original small [vehicle] regressing to the great is this same "one" and differs only in name, I do not yet understand for whom—those who regress from the great—this teaching of the two cycles of Dharma and parable was intended, and what Dharma they heard to have entered [the path].

If they heard the Dharma and the Parable, why is it not called "setting out"? If they heard the *nidāna* (causal conditions), how does it differ from "not waiting for the time"? One should know that regarding the aforementioned...
Regarding these two intermediate cycles, they are considered "regressions from the Great" in comparison to the [initial] hearing of the Dharma;
this refers to those who, having entered the analogy of the first cycle, do not receive it but instead set out to study the Small Vehicle.

These individuals are, in fact, those who regressed from the Great during the third cycle—those of dull faculties due to past causes and conditions—who, by encountering favorable conditions, transformed their dullness into sharpness within both the Dharma and the analogy cycles.
As above, those with the two middle faculties enter upon hearing the Dharma through analogy; although they enter by hearing the two higher cycles [of teaching], this is not called "setting out.

As for those who study the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna), they are attached to others; this is fundamentally due to karmic conditions from previous lives. Because people receive their names based on their original state, it is said that during the two higher cycles, they are incidentally causing those who had previously set out toward the Great Vehicle to regress.

As for those who study the Small Vehicle and are incidentally caused to set out [again], such persons— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.)

Originally, those of sharp faculties among the two groups—the Dharma-parable [preachers]—encountered adverse conditions that caused their sharpness to turn into dullness, becoming like those of the third group who were only able to enter into awakening upon hearing the causes and conditions of past lives.
Although they heard the causes and conditions and entered into awakening, they do not lose the designation of "non-retrogression.
This is because they are attached to the original nature of the two groups—the Dharma-parable—and thus retain their original title. Therefore, it is so stated.
The ancillary [teaching] initiates the departure for those of lesser capacity; thus we know that karmic conditions differ and their transformations are not the same.

As stated in the *Fahua wenju* (Words and Phrases of the Lotus Sutra) regarding the clarification of the different ways the faculties transform during the three stages: "The mental consciousnesses of sentient beings are unstable;

when they encounter adverse conditions, the sharp are transformed into dull, and when they encounter favorable conditions, the dull are transformed into sharp. The person addressed here as an ancillary case is precisely like this.

The meaning of this [passage] is that their significance is extinguished and equalized. If this were so, then since setting out from the beginning in the Small Vehicle and retreating from the Great Vehicle would be identical, why does the *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy) state that within this assembly there are those who have responded to transformation by retreating from the Great Vehicle, as well as those who originally resided in the Small Vehicle? After they receive their predictions, both are fit to be part of the "congregating audience" (*saha-śrāvaka*).

Since it is said they include those who retreated from the Great Vehicle and those who originally resided in the Small Vehicle, how can they be called "identical"? This is truly because they accord with the truth.
Because the names of the assembly of listeners enumerated in the three cycles differ, there is a distinction between the two titles "regressing from the Great" and "originally Small";
yet when one investigates their fundamental nature, they are in fact one. It is evident that the initial departure was from the Small, and this text serves to encompass and clarify that meaning.

Second, regarding the investigation into whether the great elements (*mahābhūta*) exist or not: for those of definitive nature (*niyata-gotra*), do they still possess the great elements even when encountering a Buddha?

If one were to say they do not, the treatise states: "The first two, being immature, are not given a prediction. Since it says they are "immature," they must necessarily have the seeds [of Buddhahood] beforehand.

If one were to say they do have them, then regarding the third type, although the commentary on the *Śāstra* states that they merely encounter the Lesser Vehicle, [this would contradict the presence of the seeds].
The *Lun yu da miao le shi* (Commentary on Encountering Great and Sublime Joy) states: "Regarding the third type of person, who has never heard [the Mahāyāna], they immediately enter saṃsāra;

this person takes the moment of first hearing as their initial connection with the Dharma. Based on this passage, it would seem that there can be no "great elements" (*mahābhūta*). How, then, is this to be adjudicated?
The masters of old adjudicated that those of fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*) among the Śrāvakas definitely lack the great elements. Tiantai explicitly stated: "The third..."

Third, this treatise discusses only meeting with the small [vehicle] and not meeting with the great; it is clearly demonstrated that there is no "great element" (mahābhūta) by the fact that "wondrous bliss has never been heard" and "excrement immediately flows out.
The treatise states: "Those who are 'unripe' do not previously possess the seed. This so-called "unripeness" means they have not yet escaped [saṃsāra]; thus it is called "unripe.
Because those of fixed nature (niyata-gotra) do not reach liberation through the revelation of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, they are said to be unripe. If...

How does one distinguish those who possess the great elements (*mahābhūta*) from those who have regressed from the state of a Great Being? This master’s explanation is entirely confused regarding the sutra commentaries.

Since the Tiantai school divides the sutra into three sections—first clarifying the shared formation of conditions in the past, second clarifying their further meeting in the interim, and third clarifying that they are now preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*—if those of fixed nature lacked the great elements, how could this be said?
In the past, we formed a karmic connection; this was not a fixed nature, but a shared great bond for the Mahāyāna. With whom else could such a bond have been formed?

Were it not for the presence of the seed, how could we have encountered one another again in the interim? Were it not for the presence of the seed, how could the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* be preached to us today?
How much more so when, having changed our discourse, you claim that what is not yet mature is "not yet liberated"—this error is profound. Furthermore, it is because the seed has reached maturity.

To say that "liberation from the three [realms] is never abandoned from beginning to end" would conversely imply that there is only liberation while the seeds and their ripening do not exist—which contradicts the sūtras and commentaries and leads to such erroneous explanations.

What I have now determined must be understood as follows: regarding those of fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*), since the treatise states that "the first two [stages] are not yet matured," it is evident that they possess the great seeds (*mahā-bīja*);
this intent is perfectly clear. It is simply because these individuals have dull faculties (*mṛdu-indriya*) that [this distinction is made].
Because their hindrances were heavy, immediately after the seeds were sown, they transmigrated until this very day, and the seeds have still not yet ripened;
it is only now that they hear this sutra in that land. Thus, the "Parable of the Phantom City" chapter of the sutra consists of three sections.

Within the third section, "Returning to Explain the Lotus," there are further two parts: first, correlating the ancient with the present; second, properly clarifying the returning explanation of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. The first of these parts also has two sub-sections.
The first assembly concerns the masters of the past and present; the second assembly concerns the disciples of the past and present.

Among the future disciples, the first refers to those formally included in the sutra text, as it says: "After my parinirvāṇa, in the future age, there will be śrāvaka disciples. The second refers to those whose doubts are resolved by the sutra, as it says:
"After my parinirvāṇa, there will further be disciples who have not heard this sutra, and who do not know or realize that they are bodhisattvas."
Regarding their practice, they conceive the thought of extinction regarding the merits they have attained, thinking, "I shall enter nirvana.
Although these people conceive the thought of extinction and enter nirvana, they seek the Buddha’s wisdom in other lands and there hear this sutra.
This is the section on resolving doubts as interpreted by Tiantai.

This text states that were it not for those of great penetration and noble lineage, how could one today—conjoining the ancient and the modern within the land of skillful means in a future age—be able to hear this sutra?

It is because, although those who have regressed from the Great Vehicle share the same fixed nature as those of great penetration, they merely planted the seeds through the formation of karmic conditions;

whereas after those who have regressed from the Great Vehicle have planted their seeds, they subsequently hear the Perfect Dharma and, in accordance with the teaching, initiate practice in the interim.

If one becomes weary and regresses from the Great [Vehicle] to take up the Small, and if this person is of a fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*), then after the seed has been sown, they will never again hear the Dharma of the Perfect and Constant;
because they exclusively delight in the Small, the *Wenju* states: "We discuss only the encounter with the Small, not the encounter with the Great.
Jingxi further says: "This person takes their initial hearing of the Small as the first connection (*prathama-pratibandha*), and so on, until it says 'the intermediate...'"
As for the statement regarding "looking back from oneself to the original beginning when a small affinity was first formed," these are all the original beginnings of the intermediate period;

it does not refer to Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū as the original beginning. It is an error for past masters, failing to understand this, to cling exclusively to this text and claim that those of fixed nature (niyata-gotra) lack the great elements (mahābhūta).
Regarding the statement that the Tripiṭaka and Shared [teachings] pass through the eight gates:

if, according to our own school’s clarification, those of fixed nature among the śrāvakas do not reach the Vaipulya [sūtras], why does the *Myōraku* (Wondrous Joy) state that the eight gates of the Tripiṭaka and Shared [teachings] each have four kinds? Since the Shared teaching already possesses these four kinds of śrāvakas, it cannot be that those of fixed nature come to the Vaipulya.
If they do reach the Vaipulya, they must surely reach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. This was the view of the "old masters."

Some say that those of fixed nature do not reach the Vaipulya (fangděng) teachings; yet here it is said that within the eight gates of the Tripitaka and the Shared Teachings (*xiāngtōng*), each gate contains four types of persons.

These four types are not the four mentioned in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra-śāstra*, but rather the four types of persons—those of the sequential and non-sequential Buddha-ways—who are the transformations of the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) and the first abode (*prathamavihāra*).
As the *Myōraku* states: "In the eight gates of the Tripitaka and the Shared Teachings, each gate has four [types of persons]."

Each of these categories and gates possesses its own Buddha-way and traces of responsive transformation (*nirmāṇa-kāya*), which appear before us; furthermore, the teaching is the same as previously described, and its textual expression is manifest.
Some say: "This text precisely punctuates the phrases through four types of interpretation to dissolve the sutra.

Regarding the 'interpretation according to the teaching' (*yōkyō-shaku*) for clarifying the meaning, it is because the two teachings of *pitaka* (Tripitaka) and *tong* (Shared) both expound the True Truth (*satyārtha*) and their meanings regarding cultivation and realization are identical; therefore, it is said that there are eight gates for each of the *pitaka* and *tong* teachings."
The four gates are not for those of fixed nature in the Shared Teaching who have come to the Vaipulya;

yet although these two explanations each have their own intent, upon examining the text, the reasoning in both is incorrect. This is what is meant by the saying: "The world lacks men of complete talent; it is rare to possess all excellences.
Now, following the *Shu* and *Ji*, I investigate their ultimate purport: they not only differ from previous views, but also accord with [the truth].

To combine the *Zuwen* (Ancient Commentary) with the text of the *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy) and claim that the *Zang* (Tripitaka) and *Tong* (Shared) teachings each have four types is precisely a misinterpretation of the commentary’s text;
it fails to recognize that the passage lists the assembly of listeners (*sahāya*) in order to refute ancient interpretations. Why is this?

It is because this sutra lists the assembly by first listing the *śrāvakas*, next the *bodhisattvas*, and finally the miscellaneous assembly (*miśraka-parṣad*). The ancient masters judged that the *śrāvakas* delight in...

Those in *nirvāṇa* and those among gods and humans are attached to birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), each having their own partiality; the Bodhisattva, neither delighting in nor attached to either, dwells in the central terrace of the Lotus Flower, destroying both the provisional and the real.
As for those who understand [this], the Śrāvakas keep it secret within while manifesting outwardly—how could they ever take *nirvāṇa* as a fixed guarantee?

Both gods and humans are all great *mahāsattvas*; how could they again be immersed in or stained by birth-and-death? All these are provisional traces used to lead away from the two extremes, yet the fundamental reality remains constant.

This is the Middle Way. Furthermore, citing the *Dharmapada-śāstra*, it quotes the passage concerning the refutation of the four types of śrāvakas based on their abiding in the fruit through the Buddha of Response and Transformation:
"Now, 'abiding in the fruit' is divided into two: abiding in the fruit by means of dharmas is the śrāvaka of the Tripiṭaka Teaching;

abiding in the fruit by means of the essence of dharmas is the śrāvaka of the Shared Teaching. 'Response and transformation' is further divided into two: the response and transformation that has ascended to the stages is the Distinct Teaching."
When Śrāvakas ascend to the stages (bhūmis) and manifest transformation, they are Śrāvakas of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao), who open the Buddha-way for themselves.

When Śrāvakas also act as two [types of teachers] to cause others to hear the Buddha-way in succession, they are Śrāvakas of the Distinct Teaching (biejiao), causing others to hear the Buddha-way in succession.

When they cause others to hear the Buddha-way not in succession, they are Śrāvakas of the Perfect Teaching. The meaning of "Śrāvaka" is vast; how can it be proven? It is determined by the *Myōraku* (Wondrous Joy).

Even though the commentary explains that the term "vast" (*haoran*) refers to the Śrāvakas and is not a critique of their doctrine, those who employ the teachings state that Mahāyāna Śrāvakas have not yet fully understood it.

Now, when it says they are "manifested transformations" (*nirmāṇa-kāya*) explained from the perspective of the fundamental [nature], this is based on the fact that, for the assembly as a whole, they remain entirely within the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*).
As for what is meant by "vast," the *Āgama* and *Vaipulya* [teachings] each have eight gates, and within each gate there are four types. What are these four types? This is truly because...

The four types within the non-discursive [teachings] are precisely those who abide in the fruit, the transformation-buddhas (nirmāṇa-buddhas), and those with overweening pride regarding the Buddha-way;

the four types of predictions are likewise judged as being the gates of teaching, each gate having its own traces of the Buddha-way and transformation, and the preceding teachings are again the same as before.

According to the fundamental source, there are further the stages of abiding on the ground, dwelling on the ground, and the practices leading toward the ground; the confusion caused by overweening pride is again the same as the previous count. This, then, is abiding.
If one considers [the stages] as being identical, then regarding the path of the *nirmāṇakāya* Buddha, those with arrogant pride claim they can be identical to the ancients;

yet they merely speak of *śrāvakas* delighting in *nirvāṇa*, and in discussing this, they only manage to abide in the stage of the fruit (*phala*) of the present house. Although they grasp one aspect of this meaning, they lack the eye of the teaching regarding the others, and thus explain according to their own whims.
His record further refutes this, saying: "They lack the perspective of the provisional teachings (*yōkyō*), which distinguishes between the fundamental principles of the past and the present."

In the commentaries on the provisional and the real, or their opening and closing, it is simply stated that those who abide in the fruit and those who employ skillful means [are included]. Therefore, the objection is raised:
"How does this prove [the attainment of] Nirvana? The purport of the text is already evident; why must one resort to such forced interpretation?

If that were so, then those with overweening pride—who have not attained yet claim to have attained, and have not realized yet claim to have realized—could also be said to be indiscriminately included within the ranks of those abiding in the fruit, as they too manifest through transformation.

If such a person were to keep it secret while appearing outwardly otherwise, that might indeed be permissible; however, regarding the Buddha-way and the śrāvaka-way, this present sutra reveals them, causing all to hear of the Buddha-way through sound.
Since the Buddha-way exists only for those newly entering [the path], how can one say they are "again the same as the previous number"?
You should know that we are currently merely attaching names to explain the meaning in order to refute the ancients; one must not stubbornly cling to the literal text and reject [the truth].
The brilliance of their debates over textual meaning is as radiant as the sun and moon; yet, like those born blind who do not see them, they give rise to heterodox views.

Ancient scholars already identified the four categories of the *zang* (Tripitaka) and *tong* (common) teachings as the four types within the treatises, yet to claim that these obstruct the fixed nature [of the Śrāvaka] and then to apply this to the Vaipulya (fangdeng) teachings—how crude and base this is!
Fourth, showing the purpose of the text and resolving doubts regarding obstacles: The first two cycles were for those who were secondary;

these individuals were originally of the third cycle, possessing extremely dull faculties, but because they encountered favorable conditions, their dullness was transformed into sharpness. Furthermore, those who were temporarily directed toward the "City of Illusion" (the Hīnayāna) were also secondary;
although they were originally people of the first two cycles, because they encountered adverse conditions, their sharpness was transformed into dullness. If this is so, then as for the Dharma...

Question: How can there be adverse conditions (*pāpaka-pratyaya*) while seated upon the lotus throne? Answer: This refers, in the near term, to the period prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, and in the distant term, to the period after the formation of karmic connections during the *Mahāvaipulya-mahāsannipāta*.
How could it be that one encounters adverse conditions only upon reaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*? Question:

If you claim that those of fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*) do not reach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, why does the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* state: "At that time, the Buddha addressed Pūrṇa and all those in the assembly who were still subject to outflows..."?
All Arhats who have exhausted their training, today the Tathāgata has universally proclaimed for this assembly the true nature of the ultimate meaning within the ultimate meaning,

The *Dacheng miyan jing* (Great Profound Mysteries Sutra) states: "Those śrāvakas of fixed nature have long practiced distinct roots of goodness.

Thus, one immediately enters the cycle of rebirth; though the duration of practice in the Lesser Vehicle may differ—whether long or short—it remains distinct from the roots of goodness of the Mahāyāna.

As for those śrāvakas with overweening pride, they indeed can be born in the Land of Expedient Means and attain liberation. The *Lengqie sanji* (Three Records of Laṅkā):
The words are obscure and the meanings are profound; our Patriarch left no written commentary, and Jingxi’s exposition was brief. Teachers lack sufficient insight, and students rarely understand.
As I have investigated this sutra, it is truly difficult to penetrate its depths; were it not for the transmission of a master, how could one find the proper method?
Now, following what has been transmitted, it is necessary to transcribe this so as to provide for the descendants' legacy, thereby causing the empty chamber to give birth to radiance.
This is divided into four parts: first, presenting the text; second, raising doubts and difficulties; third, providing detailed explanations; and fourth, resolving remaining obstacles.

First, regarding the presentation of the text: the *Fuxing* (Supplementary Practice) states that throughout all teachings prior to the *Lotus Sūtra*, there is no textual passage indicating that those of the Two Vehicles attain Buddhahood, nor is there any teaching clarifying that the Tathāgata attained enlightenment long ago.
Therefore, we know that this is because [those earlier teachings] were all accompanied by provisional means (*upāya*).

If this were not the case, how could it be that only the *Vaipulya* (Perfect and Subtle) section excludes the Two Vehicles? Question: If you say that the *Vaipulya* period does not record the attainment of Buddhahood for the Two Vehicles...
For what reason, in the second chapter of the *Laṅkāvatāra*, the "Transformation Chapter," does Mahāmati ask the Buddha why the Tathāgata bestows predictions of enlightenment upon the śrāvakas?
The Buddha replies that he grants these predictions for three reasons: first, to secretly encourage those who have entered the realm of nirvana without remainder to practice the bodhisattva path;
second, to urge those bodhisattvas in this world or other lands who delight in seeking the nirvana of a śrāvaka to abandon such a pursuit.
Because they cultivate great practices with their minds, the three transformation Buddhas bestow predictions upon śrāvakas; it is not the Dharma-nature Buddha who does so (and so forth).

In the first chapter of the *Lankavatara Sutra*, within the assembly of the Vaipulya scriptures, during the "Chapter on Transformations," the Tathagata exhorts bodhisattvas of dull faculties and encourages them to practice the bodhisattva path.

If one asks, "What is meant by 'co-residing' (tongju) when it refers to entering the realm of no-remainder (anupadhiśeṣa-dhātu)?"—if one investigates and interrogates this matter thoroughly, it is truly difficult to comprehend. How, then, can this be explained and reconciled?
Regarding the threefold detailed explanation, it does not go beyond two points: first, to correctly record the fulfillment of the secret prophecy and to manifest encouragement.

This is because, prior to the *Nirmāṇa-parivarta*, although the Tathāgata secretly conferred a prophecy upon the Bodhisattva Mahāmati, the śrāvakas were neither present in the assembly nor did they hear or know of it;

At the beginning of the "Chapter on Transformations" (*Nirmāṇa-parivarta*), there was no occasion for a question to be raised;

rather, it was a secret bestowal of predictions upon the śrāvakas intended to urge on the dull-witted bodhisattvas to cultivate the bodhisattva practice. It is clear that the śrāvakas themselves did not understand this. Thus, the *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) states:

The words of exhortation have now become twofold: if it concerns a Bodhisattva, one should exhort them to resolve upon the Great Mind and not retreat from the practice of Bodhi;

therefore, it is so. As for what was said regarding entering the realm of no-remainder while practicing the path of a Bodhisattva, this is the same.

This refutation is now presented with its underlying intent, which is not without reason.
As stated in the first point, for the sake of those entering the realm of nirvana without remainder, the Tathāgata secretly exhorted them to cultivate the bodhisattva path.

Since the Tathāgata had thus exhorted the śrāvakas of dull faculties in the *upāya-kṣetra* (convenient land) to cultivate the bodhisattva path, they consequently harbored doubts, thinking: "What I have realized cannot be the ultimate truth."

In truth, what would be the purpose if the Tathāgata, having already attained ultimate realization, were to encourage those of the two vehicles within the *upāya*-land to practice the Mahāyāna? Therefore,
it is precisely for the sake of rebuking and disparaging those who are ashamed of the Small Vehicle and aspire to the Great,

as well as for the sake of encouraging Bodhisattvas in this realm and other lands who delight in seeking the *śrāvaka*’s nirvāṇa to abandon such a mind and cultivate the Great Practice, that the Tathāgata [acts in this way].

Having thus exhorted the bodhisattvas of dull faculties in this land and those in other realms who have regressed from the mind of enlightenment—urging those who delight in the practice of śrāvakas not to give rise to such a mind and instead to advance in the Great Practice—he taught that the Dharma of the Two Vehicles is not ultimate.
When the śrāvakas heard this teaching, they immediately became doubtful, thinking: "The Dharma I have realized, I myself claimed to be ultimate."

Now, as for these bodhisattvas who seek nirvana, the Tathāgata exhorts them not to give rise to such a mind, but rather to cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva, thinking, "That which I have realized is not yet the ultimate.
Consequently, they come to feel shame for the small and aspire to the great. Although this is called "exhorting and advancing" the bodhisattvas, it is in fact a "displacement" of the śrāvakas.
This refers to the three types of transformation buddhas who bestow predictions upon śrāvakas; it does not refer to the buddhas of the dharma-nature.
A manifested Buddha must rely on the protection of the Vajrapāṇi to bestow predictions upon śrāvakas;

If even the Buddha who grants the prediction is not ultimately real and requires protection, how much less can the person being predicted be real? Thus, he harbors such reflections regarding both possibilities.
The meaning should be refuted by clarifying this: it not only accords with the Buddhist sūtras, but also deeply conforms to the intent of the Patriarchs.

Since the sutra clearly employs censure and rejection [of other teachings], Tiantai judges them as having the meaning of "Vaipulya penetrating the later period. If that is so, why is this?

This is because it clarifies the dharma of emptiness within the Vaipulya (*Vaipulya-sūtra*) scriptures; for this reason, it can be called *Prajñā*.
[The previous section] was at the beginning.

Although the emanated bodies (nirmāṇakāya) appear diverse, these emanated bodies originate from the wondrous section of the present sutra and are not what was discussed in the teachings of the past; this is because they pertain to the provisional traces (traces).
The three cycles of the provisional gate’s revelation of the transformative deeds having been completed, the primary gate now sweeps away the traces to reveal the fundamental; this is about to arise.

Therefore, within the circulation of the provisional gate, the jeweled stupa emerges to certify that the provisional was opened to reveal the real, and to trigger the subsequent primary gate’s revelation of the fundamental.
It is because the dispersed emanations were previously gathered, and only then was the stupa opened, in order to manifest that the Tathāgata has long [resided in the world].
If it were accomplished only now, how could there be emanated bodies? Since the emanated bodies have already gathered, Bodhisattvas surge forth before them;
from this movement, Maitreya conceives a doubt regarding their proximity, and subsequently, he is moved to hear the Tathāgata discourse upon their distant origins.
Therefore, Jingxi (Zhiyi) said: "The gathering of emanated bodies to summon the original [body] serves to manifest that Śākyamuni is not newly accomplished. Thus it is.

The intent of this principle—whether it pertains to the past or the present, and whether it is universal or limited—is somewhat difficult to comprehend. Now, wishing to clarify and elucidate it, I shall divide the discussion into four sections:
first, showing the difficulty; second, setting forth the refutation; third, the present intent; and fourth, the analytical selection.
First, regarding the objection concerning the "emanated bodies" (分身): Are these restricted solely to the present sutra, or do they also apply to the teachings of the past?

If they apply to the past, why does the *Zhuan* (Commentary) state that the *Avataṃsaka* only mentions "principal and attendant retinues," and the *Mahāsaṃnipāta* lacks any mention of "emanated bodies"?

Furthermore, the *Prajñāpāramitā* only states that "a thousand Buddhas share the same name, Śākyamuni," and likewise never speaks of "emanated bodies. Therefore, we know that it is only in the present sutra that the term "emanated bodies" is used.

Because the traces [of the teaching] conceal the fundamental [reality], it is for this reason that it is not spoken of. If one does not understand the ancient scriptures, why does the *Ratnavyuha Sūtra* state:
"At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha first sat beneath the tree, and the hundred-billion-fold emanations of Śākyamuni Buddha were all present therein"?
Furthermore, the *Śūraṅgama Samādhi Sūtra* states: "The Bodhisattva Dṛḍhamati addressed the Buddha... even as far as the upper realms."
There are lands named "Single Lamp of Radiance" and others, all of which are manifestations of Śākyamuni; according to these ancient scriptures, he is also said to have manifested emanations.
Why, then, do you claim that this is restricted solely to the present scripture?

Next, regarding those who offer refutations: some say that the emanations in the ancient scriptures belong to the Trace Gate (Jikimon), whereas those in the present scripture belong to the Origin Gate (Honmon).

Regarding the body, some say that the *Former Sūtra* (the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*) speaks of the manifestation of emanation bodies through esoteric teaching, while the *Present Sūtra* (the *Mahāsaṃnipāta*) speaks of them through exoteric teaching;
as Jingxi [Zhiyi] says, one can understand this by reflecting on the distinction between the exoteric and esoteric intentions. Alternatively, there is a classification based on four permutations:

first, "assembled but not spoken," such as when the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* assembles [beings] in the space between the two realms, yet although assembled, they are not spoken of; second, "spoken but not assembled."
Although scriptures such as the *Avataṃsaka-alaṃkāra* and the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* speak of not gathering [the assembly], there are others that do not mention not gathering;

for instance, the various sūtras prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* both speak of and describe the gathering, as is the case with the present sūtra. However, these three explanations are all incorrect.
If one were to claim that the sūtras of the past are the "trace gate" (*jimen*) and that the emanated bodies (*fenshen*) are identical to the [original] birth, this would lead to logical fallacies.

Regarding the argument that [the Buddha] was born in another life: if he were to have been born in this very life, how could the physical substance of the four great elements—characterized by the impure outflows of the segmented birth-and-death (*paricchinna-jāti-maraṇa*)—be capable of manifesting as multiple bodies?
If, on the other hand, it refers to another life, since he only attained enlightenment at the site of Śītavane (Ji-chang) today, how can one say he was born in another life?

Furthermore, regarding the claim that the "former sutras" spoke of the manifestation of multiple bodies in an esoteric sense, texts such as the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* and the *Ratnakaranda-śrī-vyūha-sūtra* (Huayan yingluo jing) make this quite explicit.

Regarding the statement in the Sautrāntika compendium that there were "divided bodies," how could this be considered obscure? Third, concerning the inclusion [of scriptures] within the four categories:
as for the second category, which states "preached but not compiled," such as the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* and the *Ratnakaranda-śrī-vyūha-sūtra*, the *Ratnakaranda* itself explicitly states:
"The divided bodies of Śākyamuni Buddha, numbering ten billion, pervaded all therein; they all came and assembled here at this Vajra-Silent [Assembly]."

Regarding the assembly at the site of enlightenment during the period of cessation, why do you say that [the Buddha] preached there but did not gather [an assembly]? Furthermore, since the emanated bodies have already assembled, could this not be conflated with the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*?
However, these three explanations have all failed to exhaust the meaning of the emanated bodies; if one grasps the intent of the present [text], the various treatises will explain themselves.

Third, as for my current intention: there are two meanings regarding the manifestation of emanation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*). First, because the previous sutras were accompanied by provisional means (*upāya*), they could not speak of emanation bodies;
it is only because the present sutra is purely perfect and uniquely wondrous that it now speaks of emanation bodies. As the *Wenju* (Commentary on the Text) states:
"The *Mahāsannipāta* mentions 'several Buddhas granting their consent,' and the *Avataṃsaka* also speaks of several Buddhas from the ten directions preaching together."

The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, in its "Great Chapter" (*Mahāparivarta*), also states that one thousand Buddhas together preached the *Prajñāpāramitā*; yet it does not say they were all emanations (*nirmāṇakāya*) of Śākyamuni.

According to the intent of the present sutra, they must indeed be emanations; however, because they were accompanied by provisional means (*upāya*), these were not explicitly revealed during that period.

Furthermore, the *Subcommentary* (*Shu-chi*) states: "Because the traces conceal the fundamental, they do not speak of [attaining] it. This textual principle arises because the former sutras were accompanied by provisional means.

First, because the traces [of the provisional teachings] covered the fundamental [truth], the emanated bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) could not be explicitly taught; it is only now that this single, perfectly sublime sutra reveals the emanated bodies.
Second, even regarding the past sutras from the perspective of the Perfect [Teaching] itself, one may speak of its emanated bodies;

for instance, sutras such as the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda*, and the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* all speak of emanated bodies. This refers to the Tathāgata addressing those of the past who were of the Perfect [Vehicle].
The statement that it does not hinder the intent of transformation means that the first three teachings are merely expedient means; therefore, they do not involve the manifestation of divided bodies.

Ancient scholars only knew that the manifestation of divided bodies resolves the difficulty regarding the past, but they did not know that the manifestation of divided bodies fulfills the purpose of the past.

The *Huayan jing xian* (Exposition on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra) in the section on the "Fourfold Discriminatory Questions" states: "Therefore, he is able to manifest emanated bodies throughout the ten directions, all beneath the Bodhi tree-king.
Why, then, does the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Miaofa Lianhua Jing Xuan Zan) say that the *Avataṃsaka* merely mentions retinues and does not speak of emanated bodies?
Answer: Regarding the statement in the Sūtra that the "emanated bodies" (分身) are spoken of in reference to Bodhisattvas of the Perfect Teaching (圓教), the *Shu* (Commentary) states:

"The reason they are not mentioned [in other contexts] is because those [other] teachings are directed toward Bodhisattvas of the Partial Teaching (偏教) and the two vehicles of the subsequent stage; thus, they are not explicitly taught. As it is said, 'Because they still carry expedient means (方便), they are not explicitly taught during that time. Question:
If the former sūtras only spoke of emanated bodies in reference to Bodhisattvas of the Perfect Teaching, then would this not fail to apply to those of the Expedient Teaching?
Question: Why does the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* state, "The Buddha told Ānanda:

'By relying on the Buddha’s power, you are able to know this matter,'" and so forth, even mentioning that "in the direction above there is a land named One Lamp Brightness," and so on—all of which are emanations (*nirmāṇakāya*) of Śākyamuni?

If this is so, since these were spoken in the presence of Ānanda, does it mean that the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) teachings acknowledge the existence of emanations? Answer: This is because the Buddha’s power has bestowed its grace (*adhiṣṭhāna*). It is not...

One can know [this] through one's own power, as the Sūtra says: "It is by relying on the Buddha’s power that you know this matter. Since it is known through the Buddha’s empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), there is no hindrance to such knowledge.
Furthermore, according to the *Ganying zhuan* (Biographies of Resonance), twenty-one years after the Tathāgata attained enlightenment, the Buddha told Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"Go to the north of the Śrāvastī ordination platform and strike the bell to summon the monks of the ten directions," just as in the visualization.
The Bodhisattva Samantabhadra and others were all assembled, and my ten billion emanations of Śākyamuni each mounted a multi-storied pavilion and arrived at the site of the ordination platform.
If this is so, does this not contradict the teaching of emanations given to Maudgalyāyana within the Hīnayāna? However, this principle was already established previously;

it is an empowerment through spiritual power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and thus does not hinder the function of transformation. Question: In the past sutras, [emanations] were taught in relation to the Perfect Bodhisattvas...

Regarding the statement that the manifestation of the divided bodies was clearly proclaimed, do those with partial capacities know it or not? If they know, it would obstruct the intent of the transformation;
yet if they do not know, how could they not know when it was clearly proclaimed? Answer: Although it is said to have been clearly proclaimed, they still do not know.

This is because, through the inconceivable power of the Tathāgata’s three wheels, the capacity of those with partial dispositions is concealed and covered, such that they are not made to know. This is because they still carry with them the traces of expedient means.

Because it is manifest yet esoteric, Jingxi said: "The meanings of the manifest and the esoteric differ; reflect upon this and you will understand they are not the same as the ancients who did not distinguish between the partial and the perfect, treating all as esoteric teachings.
Now, that which is perfected in the Perfect [Vehicle] is manifest, while that which is perfected in the Partial is esoteric. Question:

The sutras of the past were already established for a long time as the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body), whereas at the present site of Śrāvastī, it is only now that the *nirmāṇakāya* is first established. If this is only now being established, how is it that the *puṣpa* (flower) [of the Lotus Sūtra]...?

Why is it that the *Sūtra on Adorned Necklaces* does not explain this explicitly? Furthermore, if these were only now newly formed, how could they produce the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) of such defilement and turbidity?
And if they were formed long ago, would that not obstruct the transformative activities of the Original Gate? Answer: They were indeed formed long ago and are not newly formed.
The *Wenju* (Commentary on the Words) states clearly: "The *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra* explains that various Buddhas offered their consent (*adhiṣṭhāna*), and so forth."

According to the intent of the present sutra, it should be understood that since [the Buddha] has already been reunited with the present sutra for a long time, it is clear he is a manifested body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

However, because he previously employed skillful means (*upāya*), he did not explicitly state this. If one speaks in contrast to the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*), what hindrance could there be?

Otherwise, within the current circulation of the "Trace Gate" (*jia-men*) of this sutra, since the traces have not yet been swept away to reveal the fundamental reality (*mūla*), how could the Jewel Stupa [have appeared]?
Does the teaching in this chapter—that the transformation bodies (nirmāṇakāya) were accomplished long ago—not also obstruct the transformative activities of the Honmon (the Essential Gate)? Question:

Since even the orthodox teaching of the Jikimon (the Trace Gate) in the *Lotus Sūtra* cannot speak of the fact that [the Buddha] was accomplished long ago, how could the ancient sūtras speak of transformation bodies accomplished long ago?
Answer: If it is taught in contrast to the Bodhisattvas of the Perfect Teaching who, in the past, had destroyed ignorance, then it does not obstruct the present sūtra’s Trace Gate.

After the three turnings of the wheel, although within the period of dissemination the traces have not yet been swept away to reveal the fundamental, one speaks of the long-established transformation bodies (nirmāṇakāya) in contrast to those who have destroyed ignorance during the three turnings.

Since this does not hinder the teaching of transformation bodies for Bodhisattvas of the past Perfect Teaching (Ekaprativedha-yāna) who have likewise destroyed ignorance, such transformative function is unimpeded.
If this is so, then even at the initial stage of the past, those of the Perfect Teaching knew that there are transformation bodies.

[Question: Regarding the body [of the Buddha], is it so? [Answer: No. Since those of the Initial Stage of the Perfect [Vehicle] had not yet entered reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) in the past, they were separated from the Perfect by the partial;

they did not understand the transformative function and did not know of the emanation-bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*). As for those of the past Perfect [Vehicle] who had already entered reality, they have come down to the present sutra; for them, the discourse concerns only further progress.

Those who have not yet entered reality must hear the revelation of the opening and manifestation (*ekayāna-vyākaraṇa*), and the emanation-bodies are likewise so. This is like those of the three assemblies (*trivartman*), who, although they had already entered reality, [continued until... *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.*

In the "Chapter on the Real Stūpa," it is stated that the emanated bodies (nirmāṇakāya) assemble from afar; this makes it clear that those who had previously perfected their initial resolve could not have known of the existence of these emanated bodies.
Question: Since the emanated bodies were already established long ago according to the former sūtra, how do they compare to those in the present sūtra?

If they are different, then the emanated bodies of both sūtras would have been established at different times. If they are the same, then why is it that in the present sūtra the stūpa of jewels emerges and only then do the emanated bodies assemble?

Question: Manifesting the traces to reveal the fundamental source is a remote teaching; how can it be the same as [the teachings of] An? Answer: The emanated bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) of the present and the past are the same, but there is a difference in the extent of their manifestation between the Exoteric and Esoteric.
As the *Wenju* states: "The present sutra not only has a greater number [of emanations], but also explicitly teaches that these are emanated bodies. Question:
In this sutra, only after the three transformations of the land is the emanated body established, and only upon attaining ultimate purity does the name "fangzhang" (a room of one square zhang) apply.
The room naturally accommodates thirty-two thousand lion thrones; is it not the case that the power and function of the present sutra do not equal those of the past sutras?

Answer: The intent of the transformation in these two places is different. In the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, Vimalakīrti rebukes and refutes the followers of the Two Vehicles to manifest inconceivable matters;

thus, what was narrow becomes pervasive. In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the provisional is opened to reveal the real, signifying the destruction of the three delusions and the sublation of the lower three [vehicles].
The Tathāgata Fangtuan Xianruo’s expedient means for transforming beings are vast and pervasive; one should know that the intent behind his transformations in those two instances is different.
How could they be compared as being equivalent? This would surely constitute an obstacle.
[As for] the dragon girl attaining Buddhahood—

The account of the dragon girl attaining Buddhahood originates from this sutra, which manifests the efficacy of the *Miao* (Wondrous) section and reveals the power of the provisional teachings (*kaichuan*).
Although the sutra text merely states that "this very female body becomes a Buddha," the commentary (*shu*) introduces the phrase "attaining Buddhahood through the eight phases" (*baxiang chengdao*).

Consequently, it has become difficult to clarify the distinction between the fruits of retribution and habituation, and scholars since ancient times have remained unable to discern the two paths of the provisional and the real.

All are troubled by this text; now, wishing to provide a thorough explanation, I shall briefly divide it into three parts: first, showing the difficulty; second, providing the explanation; and third, making a critical selection.

First, regarding the showing of the difficulty: according to the present sutra’s prediction of enlightenment, the dragon girl immediately proceeds to the Southern World of No Defilement to achieve Buddhahood.
Is this a fruit of retribution (*vipākaphala*) or a fruit of habituation (*niṣyandaphala*)?

If it were a fruit of retribution, why did the assembly at that time see this woman suddenly transform into a man, go immediately to the Stainless World (*Vimalā-loka*) in the south, attain equal and perfect enlightenment, and preach the Dharma to deliver sentient beings?
How could she have abandoned her retribution? If it were a fruit of habituation, why did Zhiyi of Tiantai say, "In the south, the conditions have ripened"? It is appropriate [to consider it as such].
Since the attainment of enlightenment through the eight phases involves these eight phases, does he not remain in his physical retribution?
To provide a further clarification: some say that the Dragon Girl’s attainment of Buddhahood as a result of her practice demonstrates the power and function of the Sūtra; as the Sūtra says:
"In an instant, she transformed into a male and immediately went to the Stainless World in the South, where she sat upon a precious lotus flower."
Is the attainment of Equal and Perfect Enlightenment not the fruit of cultivation (*śikṣā-phala*), or is it rather the fruit of retribution (*vipāka-phala*)?

As Tiantai stated regarding the maturation of conditions in the South, "it is appropriate to attain the Way through the eight phases. Since there are these eight phases, is it not indeed the fruit of retribution?

However, these two views each grasp only one side and are not entirely satisfactory; I am merely taking advantage of the situation while the two sides—like the sea eagle and the clam—are preoccupied with their mutual destruction.
Now it must be understood that because a single dragon girl attained equal and perfect enlightenment, the faculties and perceptions of those in the two lands differ.
To the great assembly of devas and humans at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* assembly here, this woman was seen as having attained equal and perfect enlightenment in her very body;
yet for those in the South, the karmic conditions were such that they saw her cast off this retribution body and attain the Way through the eight phases of manifestation. This is because...
Because their perspectives and insights differ, Tiantai stated that the conditions here in this land are thin, whereas the conditions in the South are ripe for the Dragon Girl’s teaching;
it is appropriate that she should achieve Buddhahood through the eight phases of enlightenment. Since the meaning of these words is clear, why trouble oneself with bitter contention?

Third, the threefold selection of questions concerns whether the Dragon Girl’s attainment of Buddhahood is provisional (*upāya*) or real. If it were provisional, it would not manifest the power and function of this sutra;
if it were real, why does the *Miaole* (The Wondrous Joy) state that the passage concerning the Dragon Girl is spoken from the perspective of the provisional? Answer:

Since Jingxi states, "The passage concerning the Dragon Girl here is spoken from the perspective of the provisional," it is provisional and not real. Although the Dragon Girl is provisional, [the teaching] is provisional...

Because it must necessarily lead to the reality [of the fruit], the *Myōraku* (Wondrous Joy) states: "This refers to what is called 'the practice of reality does not hasten, while the practice of expedient means merely leads [to the goal]'.

Furthermore, it says: "Since the conditions in the south have matured, one should manifest the path through the eight phases of enlightenment. If this were the practice of reality, then [the Dragon Girl] would be a mere beast;
why then would it say that "the conditions in the south have matured"? Question: When the Dragon Girl attains Buddhahood in the south, does she still bestow the teachings of the five periods? If...
If one gives these five offerings, the great assembly in this seat sees this woman go to that land to universally expound the wondrous Dharma for all sentient beings throughout the ten directions;
yet if one does not give these five offerings, although the eight signs are present, why is it that the five offerings are absent?
Answer: This is also because the capacities and perceptions of those in the two lands differ. Now, in this Lotus Sutra assembly, there are gods and humans...
Because the multitude saw the birth of the Buddha and he immediately preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, it is said that he "expounded the wondrous Dharma.
If those in that land perceive the eight phases [of a Buddha's life], this is still what is seen as the bestowal of the five periods of teaching.

Question: Is the Land of No Defilement a pure land or an impure land? A pure land should not have the attainment of enlightenment through the eight phases; yet why is an impure land given the name "Land of No Defilement"? Answer:
Since the efficacy of the five periods of teaching has already been demonstrated as not being that of a Pure Land, we shall for now associate this with the Dragon Girl;

because she attained perfect enlightenment in this very body characterized by the five obstacles, it is called "Stainless" (Vimalā). Question: Why does the Dragon Girl’s attainment of Buddhahood lack a specific title?
Answer: It is not that there is no specific title; the translators have merely omitted it. Alternatively, some say her specific title was "Flower Immortal" (Huaxian).
I have not yet examined the sūtras and śāstras regarding this. It is asked: When the dragon girl speaks the verses, is she praising the Buddha or praising herself?

If it were praising herself, the principle would be untenable; if it were praising the Buddha, the commentary on the sūtra does not clarify this. The answer is: Upon investigating the intent of the sūtra and its commentary, it is not that she is praising the Buddha.

This is because after the dragon girl hears the teaching of the "opening and revealing" (the *Lotus Sūtra*), she deeply realizes her own nature as well as the nature of the ten directions, including both sin and merit.

The marks [of the Buddha] are the fulfillment of the primary and secondary characteristics (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana) of the two bodies—the True Body (dharmakāya) and the Response Body (nirmāṇakāya)—attained through her own practice.

Therefore, she utters a verse to praise these very marks. Tiantai’s commentary states: "The first two lines clarify that by upholding the sutra one attains understanding; the latter two lines clarify the accomplishment of the two bodies.
According to the meaning of this text, it is clear that the Dragon Girl praises the marks of what she has realized through her own realization. Question: Regarding the womb...

Question: In the sutra, it is said that the daughter of Māra, Brahmā, and Śakra attained Buddhahood in her very body as a woman in the past; yet now, in this marvelous sutra, why does she transform from female to male? Is it not the case that the present is inferior to the past? Answer: It does not go beyond three meanings: first, because she must temporarily conform to one of the ten titles [of a Buddha], namely "Tamer of Men" (Puruṣadamyasārathi), she must undergo this transformation; second, because the dragon girl was an animal, she must [transform]; third, [because she must manifest] the marks and characteristics of a Great Man (Mahāpuruṣa). Therefore, she transforms from female to male. Furthermore, although the dragon girl attained Buddhahood in her very body in the past, she did not manifest the marks and characteristics of a Great Man; thus, she transformed into a male body to manifest those marks and characteristics.
