Now, wishing to clarify this, I shall divide it into four parts: first, the textual sources and their purport; second, distinguishing the essence during the Buddha’s lifetime; third, distinguishing the essence after his parinirvāṇa; and fourth, a critical examination to resolve doubts.

Regarding the meaning of the passage cited at the outset, the *Huayan shu* (Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra) states that within both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, four factors are universally clarified:

first, sound; second, name; third, phrase; and fourth, letter. While there are differences regarding what is accepted or rejected, there are three theories concerning "name. Regarding the three [theories] of the Hīnayāna, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* asks:
"What constitutes the essence of such Buddhist teachings? One theory holds that verbal action (*vākkarman*) is the essence; this refers to vocal sound. Second...

It is said that names and so forth constitute its essence; this refers to the collection of names (*nāma-kāya*), the collection of phrases (*pada-kāya*), and the collection of phonemes (*vyañjana-kāya*).
For a detailed account, one should consult the relevant texts. Furthermore, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "The true essence of the teaching in this land is purity found in sound and hearing;

those who wish to enter *samādhi* all do so by entering through hearing. Moreover, the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "The Dharma-aggregates spoken by the Muni number eighty thousand; their essence is speech, or..."
Their names are all subsumed within the aggregates of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

Next, regarding the World-Honored Buddha’s discernment of their essential nature: if one were to discuss this land in contrast to the lands of the ten directions, every atom is none other than the Buddha-work, and every faculty is capable of awakening and entry.
Because faculties differ in sharpness or dullness and preferences vary, the karmic conditions of those in this region for the most part follow [the following].
The auditory faculty is the sharpest among the sense organs and is thus most suitable for this purpose; because the other faculties are dull, beings have a particular fondness for hearing sounds.

Each follows the customs of their own region and accords with what is appropriate for them—whether it be contemplating with fixed eyes, smelling fragrances, or perceiving tactile sensations—all six objects of the senses (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) can lead one to realize the Way.
Although the methods of entering the Way differ according to region, the teaching-body (*śāstrakāya*) discussed here is in every case identical.

First, regarding the essence of the teaching (*śāsana-tattva*), there have been two differing traditional positions since ancient times. First, the masters who prioritize vocal action (*vāg-karman*) maintain that the single reality of sound (*svara*) is the essence;

they hold that the three provisional designations (*tri-prajñapti*) are merely the Buddha’s functional activity and cannot serve as the essence because they cannot reveal [the truth] to sentient beings.
Second, the masters who prioritize names and phrases (*nāma-pada*) take the three provisional designations as the essence, while the single reality of sound merely serves as their basis.

Because they are mutually dependent causes, it is said that speech gives rise to names, and names are able to manifest meanings; thus, [names] cannot have material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) as their essence.
These two views each cling to one extreme and consequently fall into biased conceptualization.

One should know that the essence of the teaching must be a single reality, wherein the three provisional [factors] and the four dharmas harmoniously combine to constitute its essence. Therefore, the *Myōryaku* (Wondrous Joy) states: "The term 'harmonious combination' is not [to be taken]..."
This point is a matter of debate; as the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* evaluates the merits and demerits, it states that "the two masters differ in their arguments.
Now, according to the *Nyāyānusāra*, both masters' positions are accepted. Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra-ṭīkā* says: "Examining the two preceding views, each has its own basis;
all treatises contain the principle of having two conditions, and I have never heard of a definitive judgment being made in the West [India]."

The tradition holds that [the teaching] is complete and without deficiency. Why is this? If we rely on the teaching to encompass sentient beings, there is nothing other than sound by which they may hear it;

if we rely on the teaching to seek its ultimate meaning, there is nothing other than names by which it may be manifested. Although the substance of the teaching generally encompasses all six sense objects, when sought according to its fundamental nature, it specifically takes sound as its substance.
As the *Myōryaku* (Wondrous Joy) states: "Although there are physical scriptures [in the form of] color-form after the extinction [of the Buddha]..."

Even down to names, phrases, and the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), including pure names, fragrant food, and the realization through contemplation of the practice of the Dharma—all these take the vocal teaching from the golden mouth as their fundamental basis.
From this, one knows that the essence of the teaching is a synthesis of one reality and three conventionalities upon the sensory object of sound.
Miaole further states: "If even a single character or a single sound were to be grasped by both the visual and auditory consciousnesses..."

If they do not coexist, then names, phrases, and syllables would all fail to be established; for these three are all constructed through the modulations of the Tathāgata’s golden mouth and Brahma-sound.
If they were substantially real, they would be subsumed under the category of "non-obstructive yet non-visible matter" among the three types of matter in the Abhidharma.
Regarding the determination of the essence after the three types of cessation, it likewise does not depart from the essence consisting of one reality and three conventionalities.
However, while the "one reality" differs from that of the Buddha’s era, the "three conventionalities" are no different from those of the Buddha’s era.

This is because during the Buddha’s era, sound was the "one reality," whereas after his passing, form became the "one reality"—namely, the yellow scrolls and red axes [of the scriptures]. This would be the case if the collection [of the teachings] had not yet been finalized after his passing.

Although the previous Brahma-sound has ceased, the three—name, phrase, and syllable—are placed within Ānanda’s aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) and aggregate of mental formations (saṃskāra-skandha);

it is only through their subsequent compilation that they acquire the characteristics of paper and ink. Therefore, the *Myōraku* states: "Some do not allow for the existence of physical scriptures after the Buddha's extinction, asserting that there are only names;

[they claim] phrases belong to the aggregate of mental formations. If one were to entirely deny the existence of visual scriptures, then at the very beginning [of the sūtras], 'I have heard' (*śruta*) should necessarily be changed to 'I have seen' (*dṛṣṭa*)."
The meaning of this is that although there are differences after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the three provisional designations (*prajñapti*) themselves have no distinction.

The fourfold analysis (*catur-vicaya*) explaining doubts and questions is as clarified above; it can be seen directly within the essence itself. [Question: I do not yet understand what is being pointed to as the "essence of the basis" (*āśraya-svabhāva*).
[Answer: In this present teaching, the essence of the basis is such that the phenomenon (*vastu*) is the essence of the fact, while the principle (*tattva*) is the essence of the reality.

As for what the basis is: it is the principle (li) that is revealed by means of the teaching (jiao). When the teaching has ceased, the principle remains established. Now, these expressive designations do not exceed the eight teachings;
yet these eight teachings are not separate from the one reality and three provisionalities.

By knowing this, one understands that the one reality and three provisionalities take the two principles of the True and the Middle as their basis. Question: In this land, can the sensory object of sound be discussed as being "one"?

Question: Regarding the three realities and the remaining conventional designations (*prajñapti*), can the remaining objects (*viṣaya*) also be explained? Answer: The remaining objects are also clarified. For instance, when seeing a form (*rūpa*), this is one reality;
yet that form possesses blue and yellow, which are not they are called "names" (*nāman*). This is not a "phrase" (*pada*);

as soon as there is a name, there must be a phrase, which necessarily relies upon its "syllables" (*vyañjana*). What is called syllables refers to the embellishment and manifestation [of meaning], and these also possess the three conventional designations.

This is clear. Question: During the Buddha’s lifetime, the Dharma was transmitted through sound; after his passing, it was transmitted through the written word (color/form). Why does the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary) state that "sound constitutes the Buddha-work"?

Does this mean that the principle of sound applies generally to both the period of the Buddha’s lifetime and the period after his passing? Answer: Although the Tathāgata’s Brahma-voice has ceased after his passing, the four reliances (*catur-pratisaraṇa*) continue to circulate the scriptures.
Because practitioners can hear [the Dharma] through these, it is said that the principle applies generally to the period after his passing. Question: Regarding the *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy):

It is said that some do not allow for the existence of form (*rūpa*) after the passing [of the Buddha], asserting that the *sūtra* merely consists of names (*nāman*) and phrases (*pada*), which belong to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).

If they entirely deny the perception of the *sūtra*, then at the very beginning it would be appropriate to change "heard" (*śruta*) [to "seen"]. If this is so, and you do not allow for the *sūtra* as form, then what are these yellow scrolls and red axes?
Why do you use the Buddha’s sound-objects (*śabdadhātu*) as an obstacle, yet claim that "heard" must be changed? Answer: At the beginning of the *sūtra*...
All instances of "heard" (*śruta*) should be changed [to "seen"]. If one does not allow "form" (*rūpa*), then one should not allow "sound" (*śabda*).

First, that which is apprehended by the eye and ear subsequently flows into perception (*saṃjñā*) and mental formations (*saṃskāra*); only after being compiled (*saṃgraha*) do they become textual expression.
Since neither form nor sound is permitted, if that were the case, "heard" must necessarily be changed, because sound is something that can be contrasted with form. Question: Regarding purity...
Fragrant incense, fine food, the practice of the Dharma, contemplation, and awakening—all of these take the teaching from the Golden Mouth as their foundation.
Why, then, does it say that there are those in the worlds of the ten directions who attain awakening by smelling fragrances, perceiving touch, or gazing fixedly?
How could one seek the beginning of this through vocal instruction? Why is it that this passage does not take vocal instruction as the beginning? Answer: This is because...
When comparing this land with other lands, although this land possesses the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), those who awaken to the Way here seek their fundamental source through vocal teachings.
Although in other lands one may awaken to the Way amidst the various sense objects, they do not rely on vocal teachings as the initial means.
Therefore, it is said: "How could one seek its origin through vocal teachings?"

The meaning of "one Buddha attaining enlightenment while another Buddha attains enlightenment" is difficult to clarify. Although predecessors have investigated it, they have never reached its superficial principles.
On a day of leisure, while reading the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, I happened upon this passage; having gained a thorough understanding of its intent, I have carefully transcribed it.
I entrust this to future worthies so that their minds may not harbor doubt and the text may remain free of obstruction. Regarding a long-standing uncertainty:

it has been said that only one Śākyamuni Bodhisattva attained enlightenment upon the Vajra Terrace, yet there are four different accounts of this. Why, then, does the *Myōraku* (Wondrous Joy) commentary state:
"Some say that all Buddhas of the three periods attain the Unsurpassed Way at the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, and these are distinct Buddhas"?
If it were indeed as you suggest, how could one distinguish between the Buddha’s attainment of enlightenment on the Vajra Terrace in Akaniṣṭha Heaven and [his attainment] elsewhere?
Because of this single passage, doubts have arisen in competition. Some respond:

"It is simply that the same Buddha attained enlightenment on the Vajra Terrace, yet sentient beings with different capacities perceive him as being in Akaniṣṭha Heaven; since their perceptions differ, there is no need for reconciliation."
To make such a judgment is truly a false statement; its underlying intent has not been perceived. Now, I shall set forth the correct principle so that its error may become evident.
One should know that, speaking in terms of ultimate reality, the enlightenment of the four Buddhas all occurred upon the adamantine terrace.

As for the statement in the *Myōryaku* (The Joyful Land) that they "all attained the Unsurpassed Way at the Akaniṣṭha Heaven" and that these are "the characteristics of distinct Buddhas," this is merely an attachment to the path of the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavahāra*).
The ten stages (*bhūmi*) are correlated with the celestial realms as taught in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:
the first stage is correlated with the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājakāyika*), up to the tenth stage, which is correlated with the Akaniṣṭha Heaven. As that sūtra states:
"The supernatural powers and wisdom of the tenth Stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*) cannot be fully described," and so on, until it says: "A bodhisattva dwelling in this stage..."
He frequently manifests as the Heavenly King Maheśvara; furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-ṭīkā* states:
"Mahādeva is none other than Maheśvara, who dwells at the summit of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) and presides over the trichiliocosm. A Bodhisattva of the tenth stage manifests his traces therein.
Examining this thoroughly, the ten stages correspond to the heavens such that the tenth stage precisely coincides with the Akaniṣṭha Heaven (*akaniṣṭhabhavana*), which is the distinct Buddha.

The station of the "Successor" (upapadya) manifests the form of a Lord of Devas; at the stage of the Dharma-Cloud (dharmameghā), one advances to sever the final grade of ignorance, thereby attaining the fruit of the Bodhisattva of Sublime Enlightenment (miāojué guǒfó) according to the Separate Teaching (biéjiào).
If this is so, should the "Successor" not refer to the single stage of Equal Enlightenment (děngjué), rather than the tenth bhūmi?
One should know that the single stage of Equal Enlightenment may sometimes exist and sometimes not; here, we take Equal Enlightenment as being included therein.

Because the Dharma-Cloud [Stage] (*dharmameghā*) constitutes the position of the "Successor" (*parivartin*), Jingxi grasped this meaning and stated that the distinct Buddha (*bhedabuddha*) achieves the Unsurpassed Way upon the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
If this is so, the *Wenju* (Textual Commentary) merely says that he alone manifests the *zhunti* (lofty special body), sits upon the lotus pedestal, and receives the office of a Buddha;
this refers to the distinct Buddha’s own awakening and awakening of others—what did Jingxi understand from this?
Regarding the intent of the sūtras and śāstras, why do they state that it is a distinct Buddha who attains enlightenment in the Akaniṣṭha Heaven? Answer:
Both the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra Commentary* state that Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage (bhūmi) dwell at the summit of the Form Realm as the Lord Maheśvara.
Furthermore, since the Dharma-cloud Stage (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*) is the position of a distinct Buddha’s successor (*kumārabhūta*), the Akaniṣṭha Heaven is designated [as his abode].

This refers to a Buddha attaining enlightenment separately. If that is so, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that those on the tenth stage, Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*), mostly become the Heavenly King Maheśvara.
Is this the Path of Teaching or the Fruit? If one asks whether there is such a person—if there were such a person—then they would merely be separate from the Cloud of Dharma;

yet how could there ever be such a person? If one says there is no such person, then while it might be acceptable for the Cloud of Dharma to be thus, where would the Lord of Heaven, Maheśvara, reside?

Regarding those who have attained the realization of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, the provisional teachings of the distinct teaching (*bhedavyavahāra-śāsana*) were expounded by the Teacher of that teaching for the sake of beings of the distinct capacity.
This was because, within the distinct teaching, there were teachings regarding the Buddha of the fruit of wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue guofo*), yet no person [to embody it].

Thus, as a *siddhānta* (established doctrine) to accommodate sentient beings and serve as a skillful means (*upāya*) to lead those of lower capacities into the stages (*bhūmi*), such a teaching was provisionally established. If Śakra Devendra were manifest and clearly present, [the situation would be different].

If a person merely cultivates the ten wholesome paths and meditative concentration, they will become a subject of heaven; if they further cultivate the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), they may become a lord of heaven.
This is what is stated in the *Miaoxuan Wenzu* and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-śūtra-vyākhyā*.
What does this have to do with the distinct teaching that the Bodhisattva Fayun came to serve as the lord of heaven?

The four prefaces to the *Xuánwén* constitute the beginning of the three sections, and these four prefaces are the most essential; they encompass the great purport of the entire scripture and summarize the causal origins of the two divisions.

The text is concise yet the meaning is abundant; the words are profound and the intent is far-reaching. If one wishes to ensure that the beginning and end are not obstructed, one must attain clear and thorough understanding through these [prefaces].

Now, to demonstrate the great principles, I shall briefly divide this into four sections: first, the inquiry; second, the critique of errors; third, the exposition of the correct meaning; and fourth, the clarification of obscurities. Regarding the first, the inquiry:

within the *Miaoxuan* (Profound Mystery), there are four prefaces. First, the "Private Record of the Origins" is the general preface by Zhangan for the two parts [of the *Fahua Xuanyi*], through which the meaning of the origins can be understood.
The latter preface is the *Xuanyanwen* (Explanatory Text on the Profound Meaning) composed by the Great Master himself.

The original preface can likewise be seen as such; however, regarding the intermediate preface concerning the King and the private preface concerning the King, the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary) points out:
"The first one is the Master’s separate preface to the sutra; the subsequent ones concerning the King were added by the recorder.
If this is so, why is the current main preface in the *Xuanyan* (Profound Meaning) called a "separate preface to the sutra"? It still seems redundant; how should this be resolved?

Second, regarding the critique of errors: the former claim that the "Preface to the Scriptural Commentary" (Jingxi ke xu) was the "Preface to a Separate Edition of the Scripture" is likely because the Great Master composed this preface at other times—perhaps when lecturing on the scripture for kings, high officials, ministers, disciples, or commoners—but it does not mean that this preface was specifically for the lecture on the *Xuanyan*.
Therefore, the compilers of the records [placed it] therein...

Regarding the beginning of the *Xuánwén* (Profound Text): since this preface does not comment upon the three divisions [of the Lotus Sūtra] but rather comments upon the five major points of profound meaning, these are grouped together at the beginning of the *Xuánwén* because their thematic categories correspond.
Furthermore, as the pen was in the hand of Zhǐchān (Zhāng'ān), there is no logical impediment to this arrangement.
The critique states: Jīngqī categorized the four prefaces of the *Xuánwén* and divided them into two sections; the first is "Private" (*sī*).

The section on the *nidāna* (causal origin) is designated as the General Preface (*sūtra-pūrvamīmāṃsā*), while the subsequent three sections are all designated as the Main Preface (*sūtra-madhyamīmāṃsā*).

As for the *Xuanwen*, what is meant by this "separate timing"? When lecturing on the sutra, why would there be such a preface? Furthermore, there are many other difficulties; I do not wish to evaluate them in detail here.
Once the *Zhengyi* (Correct Meaning) is published, their errors will naturally become manifest.

Third, regarding the correct principles: whenever one wishes to explain a meaning, one must first trace back to the original text before the intent can be seen. How could one possibly discard the root to seek for its branches?

Now, it is judged that the four sequences are all contained within the *Xuánwén* (Profound Text) and cannot be explained separately, as in the commentary on the *Qiān* (Notes), which concludes the explanation of the "Preface on Dependent Origination" by stating:
"The initial general preface is finished; next is the main preface. Since the *Xuánwén* contains three prefaces in total...

If you say that this "Preface" (xu) is merely a formal introduction to the "Profound Text" (Xuánwén), how could it be that there was a separate occasion for lecturing on the Sūtra at which this preface was delivered?

Furthermore, consider how Jingxi [Zhiyi] explained the character "king" (wáng) as meaning "arising" or "the beginning. Since the preface initiates the commencement of all the texts, it is called the "Preface-king" (xùwáng).
Now, if it is the beginning of all the texts, is it not indeed the entire "Profound Text"? Moreover, within the Master’s "Preface-king," he states: "As for the 'Sūtra' (jīng), it is external..."
The title of the work is *Xiūduluó* (Sūtra), the capital name for the holy teachings. Regarding the matters of having translations or not, they are explained as follows.

Jingxi’s commentary notes that because the teachings of the five flavors are all collectively termed "jīng" (sūtra), it is called the "collective name. This is fully detailed in the eighth fascicle, hence the phrase "as explained later.
This passage explicitly points to the single character "jīng," as explained in the eighth fascicle; thus, it is verified that this is from the Preface to the *Xuánzàn*, and not [the main text].
Regarding the preface to the sutra: if one were to say that the preface should be explained as "the matter is as previously explained," why then does it say "explained later"?

Furthermore, the two intermediate prefaces are composed so that teacher and disciple may mutually complete the text and its meaning through their interdependence; therefore, they exist and are not redundant. As the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary) states:
"From the 'Private Preface' to the end of the chapter on 'King,' the private preface by Zhizhe [Zhanran] is further divided into two parts: first, the preface."
Next, the explanation of the beginning of the preface is divided into two parts: first, a discussion of the beginning and the end; second, an explanation of the title of the sutra.

In the Master’s preface, he generally maintains that the title of the sutra encompasses both the beginning and the end. The Master [Zhiyi] holds that within the meaning of the title, the meaning must necessarily include the essence (*tattva*) and so forth;

Zhiyan (Chang’an) holds that in terms of what is taught, the teaching must necessarily include the essence and so forth. This differs from the "Explanation of Names" (*Shiming*), because since words and meanings depend upon one another, he explains it again here.

Thus, the Great Master followed the principle (*artha*); since "principle" encompasses both substance (*tattva*) and so forth, his intent was profound and hidden. Zhiyi (Zhang’an) followed the explanation (*vyākhyāna*); by expounding the five chapters, the meaning was finally made manifest.

Regarding the distinction made between the third and fourth sections, which clarify only two types of "borrowing" (jiejie), the text itself answers this by stating: "According to the text of the *Zhiguan*, one must discuss three types of borrowing. This is because the first two types of borrowing—though they borrow from the beginning to the end of a single teaching and involve the solitary borrowing of the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* respectively—both pertain to the stages of the Three Vehicles and are thus treated as a single category rather than being divided into two. [The author] comments: ... [The text continues with the analysis of the three types of borrowing. ... Regarding the first type of borrowing, it involves taking the stages of the Bodhisattva path from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and applying them to the stages of the Śrāvaka path within the *Abhidharmakośa*. This is called "borrowing the beginning and end of a single teaching" (*yijiao shizhong jie*). As for the second type, it involves taking the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and applying them to the ten stages of the Śrāvaka path within the *Abhidharmakośa*. This is called "solitary borrowing of the ten stages" (*danzhe shidi jie*). Although these two types differ in their specific applications, they are both categorized together under the heading of "borrowing from the stages of the Three Vehicles" (*sansheng wei jie*). Therefore, they are not further subdivided into two separate categories. This is why the text treats them as a single section. Furthermore, the third type of borrowing refers to taking the stages of the Bodhisattva path from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and applying them to the stages of the Bodhisattva path within the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda Sūtra*. This is called "borrowing from the same vehicle" (*tongche jie*). Since this involves borrowing from within the same vehicle, it is established as a distinct category. Thus, the total number of borrowings is three. This is the meaning of the text’s classification. It is not that the first two types are insufficient; rather, they are grouped together because they share the commonality of being stages belonging to the Three Vehicles. If one were to divide them based on their specific differences, there would indeed be four types. However, following the intent of the *Zhiguan*, the primary focus is on the broad categorization of the stages of the Three Vehicles, hence the establishment of three types. This is the essential point of the text's structure. It is not that the first two types are merely incidental or secondary; rather, they are fundamental to the overall framework of the stages of practice. By treating them as a single category, the text emphasizes the underlying unity of the stages across different vehicles, while still allowing for the detailed distinctions found in the original sources. This approach ensures that the practitioner understands both the shared nature of the paths and the specific nuances of each stage. Thus, the text’s treatment of the borrowings is both comprehensive and precise. It is through this careful analysis that the true meaning of the *Zhiguan*’s classification becomes clear. One must not overlook the significance of the first two types simply because they are grouped together. Their inclusion as a single category serves a specific pedagogical purpose, highlighting the structural similarities between the various vehicles while maintaining the integrity of their individual systems. This is the profound insight of the master’s commentary. To understand this is to grasp the heart of the *Zhiguan*’s methodological approach to the integration of diverse Buddhist teachings. Without this understanding, one risks misinterpreting the text’s intent and failing to appreciate the depth of its synthesis. Therefore, let us carefully examine the text once more to ensure we have fully grasped its meaning. Only then can we truly benefit from its guidance in our own practice. This is the final word on the matter. May all practitioners take heed. 

Tiantai’s opening of the topical sections (*kaikē*) involves only two "borrowings"; why then speak of three borrowings? This failure to investigate the opening chapter has led to this erroneous statement.

Since the first borrowing already borrows the beginning and end of one teaching for the sake of the Three Vehicles (Sanjō) in common, why would it be necessary to further borrow the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*) for the Three Vehicles in common?
This contains two errors; their fallacy will become evident upon reaching the main intent below. Now, to clarify the main intent: [The text continues with the main argument.]
Upon examining the opening sections of the chapters on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, there are four categories: first, the Tripiṭaka; second, the Shared Teaching (*pāryāya-śāsana*);

third, borrowing the names of the Distinct [Teaching] to designate the common stages of the Shared Teaching; and fourth, borrowing the names of the Distinct [Teaching] to designate the bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching.

Within this third category—borrowing the names of the Distinct [Teaching] to designate the common stages of the Shared Teaching—it states: "Fourth, borrowing the names of the Distinct [Teaching] to designate the bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching."

The passage in the *Weizhi* (位止) and *Guangming* (明文) that speaks of "borrowing" (借) refers only to two instances of borrowing. First, it borrows the beginning and end of the One Vehicle teaching for the three vehicles in common;

second, it borrows the beginning and end of the One Vehicle teaching specifically for Bodhisattvas. Since the intermediate section is not separately designated as a major heading, it is verified that this is not an instance of the [third] borrowing.
The *Zhiguan* states: "If one borrows this specific name," such a passage merely serves to judge the aforementioned borrowing of the One Vehicle teaching.

Because it establishes the stages for severing delusions from beginning to end, the *Zhiguan* states: "If one uses these specific names to judge the general stages of the three types of persons, the first stage severs the delusions of views;
the second stage severs one or two grades of the delusions of thought in the desire realm; the third stage severs six grades of the delusions of thought," and so on, concluding:
"By analogy with what precedes, this can be known. Since this is a judgment of the stages for severing delusions throughout the beginning and end of a single teaching, [it is established].
The preceding first section already borrowed specific names to encompass the general positions; the textual intent is clear and the opening chapters are manifest.
How can you erroneously claim that the three types of "borrowing" must now be clarified? I shall now point out their meanings so they may be seen with clarity.

Second, regarding the purpose of the borrowings in the *Miaoxuan*: the *Miaoxuan* relies on the "Positions" chapter to cite the *Lotus Sūtra*’s "three weeds and two trees" as an analogy to clarify [the stages].

The sixth section clearly elucidates the stage of the "small tree," which is precisely the stage of the three vehicles (*triyāna*) of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-śāsana*). First, the ten stages common to the three vehicles are explained;
subsequently, because the names are distinct while the meanings are shared, there are passages that borrow specific names to express general principles.

Regarding this, the *Miaoxuan* (The Profound Meaning) clarifies the borrowing; however, the intent behind its opening chapters—namely, the first and second instances of borrowing—is somewhat difficult to comprehend. Former scholars have judged that the *Miaoxuan*... [text continues].

There are thus two instances of "borrowing" explicitly stated within the text: first, the distinct name "patience" (*kṣānti*) is established for Bodhisattvas within the common stage of the Three Vehicles, yet its meaning extends beyond this;
this is the first instance of borrowing. Second, the name of the Distinct Teaching is used [for the Common Teaching], such that the name is distinct while the meaning is common;

this is the second instance of borrowing. The first is a single borrowing of the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*), wherein the name "patience" is specifically established for Bodhisattvas within the common stage of the Three Vehicles.

The sequence of names borrows from one [source] to clarify that, from beginning to end, the establishment of the name "patience" (*kṣānti*) is solely for the sake of Bodhisattvas; thus it is clear that both borrowings are made for this purpose. Critique:

This is merely a product of arbitrary speculation. Now, I shall set forth the truth so that there may be no further doubt or obstruction. Upon examining the opening chapter, there is in fact only one borrowing. Why is this so?

Initially, within the stage common to the three vehicles (*triyāna-sādhāraṇa-bhūmi*), the term "patience" (*kṣānti*) is established specifically for bodhisattvas; however, its meaning extends throughout this entire section.
This is precisely what is meant by establishing "patience" specifically for bodhisattvas within the stage common to the three vehicles according to this teaching. It is not merely a single instance;

rather, by borrowing the terminology of a subsequent section—the specific teaching (*pratyeka-śāsana*)—to name it, while the meaning remains general, this is what constitutes the principle of "borrowing. As the text states: "Second, using specific names."
The term "penetrating" (*tong*) refers to the names of the ten stages of faith, the thirty minds, and the ten grounds.

Regarding the meaning of "penetrating" in the context of the Iron Wheel stage, it refers to the Dry Wisdom Ground (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi*) and the patience of subduing (*vinīlaka-kṣānti*). The thirty minds correspond to the Stage of Nature (*gotra-bhūmi*) and the patience of compliance (*anuloma-kṣānti*), and so forth.
This is precisely what clarifies that one borrows specific names to apply them generally; examining it through this lens, there is only this single instance of borrowing.
This is certainly contrary [to your position].

this is borrowing the beginning and end of one teaching for what is shared by the persons of the Three Vehicles. Furthermore, in the *Miaoxuan*, the name of the Separate Teaching is used where the meaning is universal; this too is borrowing.

Since his nature was such that he was fit to hear the Dharma of the beginning and end of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*), the Buddha immediately expounded it for him, condescending to accord with his specific capacity.

The sixteen moments of mind for the second stage constitute the third stage; these three stages all involve the cessation of the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-heya*) without emerging from meditative absorption.

The four Patiences (*kṣānti*) constitute the first stage, the four Knowledges (*jñāna*) constitute the second stage, the subsequent Patience (*anvaya-kṣānti*) constitutes the third stage, and the subsequent Knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) constitutes the fourth stage.

These four stages all involve the cessation of the delusions of view without emerging from meditative absorption. Both [the Śrāvaka and Bodhisattva paths] rely upon this single teaching for their beginning and end.
Question: Why do the stages through which one passes while severing views differ? Answer: Because the sources differ and there are variations in the capacities of practitioners (*indriya*).

If, according to the *Miaoxuan*, one severs views by passing through only a single stage, this is derived from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. As the *Miaoxuan* cites the sūtra as proof, it first demonstrates its meaning:

the "stage of the eight persons" (*aṣṭamaka-bhūmi*) is precisely the first stage, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), because one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: [The text continues with the citation from the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra.]
Whether it be the wisdom or the abandonment of a *srotāpanna*, these constitute the Bodhisattva’s patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

If one possesses both cessation (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) and traverses the third and fourth stages, this also emerges from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. There are differences regarding whether the root-nature (*indriya*) is fixed or unfixed;

the *Miaoxuan* (Exquisite Profundity) states that those who abandon views at the first stage possess a fixed root-nature, whereas those whose cessation and insight traverse the third and fourth stages are persons of unfixed [root-nature]. As stated in the *Fuxing* (Supplementary Practice): [text follows].

Regarding the statement that "the four specific names apply generally to the stage of a Bodhisattva," this refers exclusively to the Bodhisattva; therefore, the cultivation of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) and the severing of views (*dṛṣṭi*) are not fixed.

Question: Regarding the clarification that the specific names are applied generally to the correct usage, some ancient masters held that one severs the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) at either the third or fourth stage (*bhūmi*).
Why, then, does the *Miaoxuan* (The Profound Meaning) refute these ancient masters?
The Master said: "In the Teaching of Penetration (Tongjiao), the stage of insight is fundamentally the path of non-interruption (*anantara-mārga*).
Since one realizes the fruit of Srotāpanna without emerging from meditative contemplation, how could it be that the views are severed at the first ground, or even at the third or fourth ground?

The ancient masters also used the third or fourth ground to sever the views, which is the same as our present school. For what reason does the Great Master completely disallow this? Answer: Our school... [text continues]

Although it is said that one passes through the third and fourth stages by borrowing the terminology of the "Shared" (Tong) teaching, this refers to the severing of views; yet this is actually the distinct teaching (*biejiao*).

The three and four stages, such as the Stage of Joy (*Huanxi*), are fully explained in the *Zhi Guan* (Stopping and Seeing). When these are taught solely for the sake of Bodhisattvas, they borrow the terminology of the Middle Way.

Those of antiquity did not understand this and claimed that within the Shared Teaching itself, the three and four stages—such as the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*Ganhui*)—sever views. Since the meaning of what was taught...

Now, because the sequence of stages in the *Miaoxuan* (The Profound Meaning) differs from that of the [Tiantai] teachings, there is this incongruity; therefore, the *Miaoxuan* itself refutes it, saying:

"In the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*), the stage of 'seeing' (*jian-di*) is fundamentally the path of the 'uninterrupted' (*wujian*). One does not emerge from contemplation to realize the fruit of *srotāpanna*;

how then could one sever the delusions of 'seeing' at the first ground, or even at the third or fourth ground? Since the ancients did not harmonize the Shared Teaching with its own specific doctrine, [the objection] is untenable.

The [opponents] argue that because the abandonment of views in the third and fourth stages of wisdom involves exiting meditative contemplation (*vyutthāna*), these two faults exist; therefore, their position is what is being refuted.

How could this be the same as our current [position]? Question: The abandonment of views in the third and fourth stages is precisely the shared (*sāmānya*) *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* of the present teaching.

Why then do you judge it by borrowing the names of the specific (*viśeṣa*) [teachings] to apply them to the shared, and thereby criticize the ancients? Answer: This master does not understand the intent of the sūtras. What I am saying now is based on the sūtras...

This is merely using a distinct meaning to clarify the general principle. If that is so, since you do not admit that the ancient masters held that the Shared Teaching (Sādhāraṇa-yāna) uses two stages to sever the afflictions of views, and our own school now clarifies that the Shared Teaching uses both the third and fourth stages to sever the afflictions of views, how does this differ from the ancient masters' method of severing delusions?
Answer: In our own school, if we discuss it according to the specific teaching of the Shared Vehicle itself, it is precisely the third and fourth stages that sever [the afflictions of views].
Regarding the view that the *Śrāvakabhūmi* and *Pratyekabuddhabhūmi* (the "Stopping and Contemplation" sections) borrow specific names to apply them generally—that is not correct.

In this teaching, the two stages of the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*) and the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) correspond to the eighth stage and the stage of seeing (*darśana-bhūmi*) in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*. From the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) up through the third and fourth stages, these are specific names borrowed for general application.
Ancient scholars did not understand that this sūtra borrows specific names for general application; they erroneously judged it to be a general [application].

When [the opponent] attempts to teach through the conventional *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, [the author] immediately refutes it, saying: "How does one know that this master does not understand the meaning of the sutra?

It is because he borrows specific names to apply them to the general text. Thus, the *Fuxingji* (Sub-commentary) clarifies: "If [the stages] definitely belonged to the general [vehicle], they should not be established as 'hidden positions' (*fuwei*) prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*).

If they definitely belonged to the specific [vehicle], then the stages of practice (*prayoga*) and approach (*abhimukha*) would belong to the four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), and even up to the fourth ground, they would be shared [with the general vehicle]."

The Sūtra states that the afflictions of the view-realm are severed in this manner; this is an instance where a specific name is used to refer generally [to all afflictions]. The ancient masters judged this to belong to the *dharmatā* teaching (the teaching of the present), and it is for this reason that it is refuted here.
Second is the habitual tendency (*vāsanā*).
To begin with, regarding the term "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*), it refers to the residual traces of the fundamental afflictions (*anuśaya*);

this has already been clearly explained in detail in the various sutras and śāstras concerning their names, meanings, essences, and characteristics. Although the literary compositions of various schools are diverse and all take the practices of the three families as essential, they have yet to reach the profound source of the principle of "the two being identical.
Herein, I shall briefly set forth my limited views, dividing them into three parts.

First, the clarification that the *pāṃśu* (dust-like) delusions are themselves *vāsanā* (habitual tendencies). Second, the clarification that ignorance (*avidyā*) is itself *vāsanā*. Third, the selection and resolution of doubts.

Regarding the first—clarifying that the *pāṃśu* delusions are themselves *vāsanā*—there are three parts: first, the inquiry; second, the refutation of [other] views; third, the present intent. First, as for the inquiry:

since the meaning of the habitual tendencies of the three delusions has already been established, why is it further clarified here that the *pāṃśu* delusions are themselves *vāsanā*? Since the *pāṃśu*...
Since it neither induces rebirth nor obstructs the principle, why need one discuss its meaning as being "identical to habit-energy" (*vāsanā*)?

Furthermore, regarding the aspect of responding to the capacities of beings under the Tathāgata’s wheel of Dharma when the dust-like sands [of phenomena] are identical to habit-energy—what is that aspect like? Next, regarding the refutation:

the *Miaozong* (The Wondrous Pivot) states that in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, the Buddha rebukes Śāriputra, saying: "Because your fetters and habit-energies are not yet exhausted, flowers will stick to you."

Because the body fears birth and death, the five desires find an opportunity; since one already fears birth and death, one merely points to the "dust and sands" [of phenomena] as being fetters and habitual tendencies.

[The author’s] critique says: The *Jingming shu* (Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra) clearly states that when the heavenly maiden rebuked him, she said, "If one makes distinctions regarding the Buddha-dharma, it is not in accordance with the Dharma.

Since there is already making distinctions, this constitutes the delusion of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). It further states that as long as fetters and habitual tendencies are not yet exhausted, flowers will [adhere].

Because one is attached to the body, there are afflictions of volition; the meaning of this passage is clear. When Śāriputra removed the flowers, he was seeing and thinking separately—how then can you say these were "dust-like" (*rajas*) afflictions?
Third, my current intention is that the "dust-like" afflictions explained here are actually *vāsanā* (habitual tendencies).

This is stated in relation to Bodhisattvas as opposed to the Two Vehicles: from the perspective of the Bodhisattvas, these are called "dust-like," whereas from the perspective of the Two Vehicles, they are regarded as [ordinary] dust.
The explanation of them as "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*) is precisely a concealed expression (*āvṛta-lakṣaṇa*). It is like the case of the Arhat who did not recognize red salt;

that the Arhat did not recognize it was due to a concealed expression involving "dust-like sands" (*rajas-tulya*), where it was said that he did not recognize it because his habitual tendencies were not yet exhausted.

From this one knows that for Śrāvakas they are called habitual tendencies, whereas in the Mahāyāna the actual teaching is that these "tendencies" are themselves the dust-like sands, as in the Great [Sūtra].
The treatise states: "In the Śrāvaka sūtras, it is taught as 'habitual tendencies' (*vāsanā*); in the Mahāyāna, it is truly taught that 'habit' (*xi*) is itself a distinct affliction.
This is what is meant.

Next, the discussion on the identity of ignorance (*avidyā*) with habitual tendencies has four parts: first, the purpose; second, raising doubts; third, divergent interpretations; fourth, the correct path. First:

Regarding the intent of this passage: as for the argument within our own school that ignorance (*avidyā*) is identical to habit-energies (*vāsanā*), it is because the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that while the Śrāvaka sūtras speak of them as habit-energies, in the Mahāyāna they are truly taught such that habit-energy is itself a distinct affliction (*paryavasthāna*). Furthermore, the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* states:

"In the Hīnayāna, habit-energy is not a primary affliction (*mūlakleśa*); in the Mahāyāna, however, it is truly taught that habit-energy is indeed a distinct affliction. This is because the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, having observed... [text fragment ends]... the [distinction].
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "If the bonds and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are not yet exhausted, flowers will adhere to the body.

For this reason, it is said that the Mahāyāna speaks of reality; whereas for those of the Two Vehicles, one merely severs the primary afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) but does not sever the habitual tendencies.
Thus, the treatise makes this statement in accordance with the pedagogical intent of both the Great and Small Vehicles, which has led to the present school [holding this view].
That scholars have maintained the theory that ignorance (*avidyā*) is itself the habit-energy (*vāsanā*) is precisely due to this point. Next, regarding those who raise doubts:
Śāriputra rejected the flowers, yet Kāśyapa rose to dance upon hearing the lute.

Since both of these individuals were moved by the specific delusions of ignorance, why was it that Kāśyapa recognized them as the pure and subtle five desires of a Bodhisattva, while Śāriputra did not? Furthermore—
Furthermore, when Kāśyapa heard the lute, he was so delighted that he rose to dance; why then did Śāriputra feel such loathing and discard the flower?
What is the reason for this difference between liking and disliking? Third, as for the interpretation:

some say that "knowing" and "not knowing" arise because sounds and forms differ—there being a distinction between those that possess discursive expression (*abhilāpa*) and those that do not. Kāśyapa’s dancing arose because the sound-object (*śabda-viṣaya*) possessed discursive expression.

Because [Mahāmaudgalyāyana] possesses eloquence, he knows that the removal of the flower by Śāriputra was due to the fact that the sensory object (rūpāyatana) lacks the capacity for verbal expression; because it lacks such expression, he does not know [the reason for his own reaction].
If the preferences of these two differ, it is due to their respective past habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). To explain:

Kāśyapa, having previously been a musician in a former life, still dances when hearing the lute in this present life; Śāriputra, having once been a venomous snake in the past, feels hatred toward the foul flower, as the poison of his resentment still remains. Next...

It is said that because the power of practice of these two men differs in depth, Kāśyapa—who has long practiced the dhūta austerities—possesses profound merit from his practice and thus knows this matter;
whereas Śāriputra, who delights only in extensive learning, still lacks the strength of practice and therefore does not know it.

If one were to judge them by their differing preferences, Śāriputra would merely be discriminating between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, which belongs to the realm of dualistic views, while Kāśyapa is otherwise.

Hearing the lute and dancing to it belongs to the realm of parting thoughts; since seeing and thinking differ, likes and dislikes must vary. These two views have been held by former masters since antiquity.
However, if one understands the meaning of the present context, this is not so.

When we reach the point below, these various stagnations will naturally be dispelled. Regarding the "four correct paths," they investigate the general purport of these two individuals; they are not [merely] superficial.
This means that the likes and dislikes of two people differ, as do their levels of understanding and ignorance.

If even Kāśyapa could rise and dance upon hearing the lute, how much more so would not just one person do so? If even Kāśyapa, who practiced the twelve ascetic dhūtas, rose to dance, how much more so would the śrāvakas?
While Kāśyapa rose to dance, the śrāvakas did likewise; however, we mention Kāśyapa now merely to use him as an illustrative example.
Regarding the ears, the *Mahā-kinnara-sūtra* states: "When a single string of song is struck, its sound vibrates throughout the great trichiliocosm;
Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, surges and sinks, rising and falling, such that all the śrāvakas rise from their seats as if performing a dance.
Since it says "all the śrāvakas," how could it refer only to Kāśyapa? If [the text] speaks of "Śāriputra removing the flower," why would it refer only to Śāriputra alone? As for the body:

Since even Śāriputra, who is foremost in wisdom, had to remove the flowers, how much more so must this apply to the other śrāvakas? When it is said that Śāriputra removed the flowers, the same applies to all the śrāvakas.
Now, the reason Śāriputra alone is mentioned is merely to serve as a starting point for the discussion, just as the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states:
"All the disciples, despite their supernatural powers, were unable to make the flowers fall. Since it says "all the disciples," it follows that the others did so as well.
How could it be that only Śāriputra understands the meaning of this passage? If they understand, they both understand; if they do not understand, they both do not understand;
if they are good, they are both good; if they are evil, they are both evil. This is because they are all moved by distinct delusions.
For now, I have cited the two foremost among the eminent—Kāśyapa and Śāriputra—as a starting point for discussion.

Regarding the third section, the *Mahā-śāstra* (Great Treatise) provides a detailed analysis to resolve doubts: "In the Śrāvaka sūtras, these are called 'habitual tendencies' (*vāsanā*); in the Mahāyāna, it is taught that 'habitual tendency' refers to the specific afflictions (*paryavasthāna*).

This is because it is spoken from the perspective of the Great Teaching’s concealment of the characteristics for those of the Two Vehicles; thus, where there is ignorance (*avidyā*), there is habitual tendency.

If this is so, why does the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* state that "dust-like sands" (*rajas*) are themselves habitual tendencies? Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "Therefore, [it is not so]... [The text here appears to be truncated].
If defiled ignorance is also called "habitual tendency" (*vāsanā*), and both of these treatises belong to the Hīnayāna, they should only discuss habitual tendencies;
how then can they discuss the identity of habit and [defilement], without contradicting the Mahāyāna treatises? Answer:

Although these two treatises belong to the Hīnayāna, since they were spoken after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* had revealed and clarified [the truth], there is no contradiction. If they were spoken during the Buddha’s lifetime, they would have been [restricted to the Lesser Vehicle].

Because it is a matter of spiritual capacity (*indriya*), one cannot say that [the flower] is identical to the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*); otherwise, it would contradict the intention of the Vaipulya sūtras to employ the concealment of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) as a skillful means (*upāya*). Question:
When Śāriputra was struck by a flower, the Tathāgata concealed the fact by saying his "habitual bonds were not yet exhausted" so that the flower would stick to his body;
yet when Kāśyapa danced upon hearing the lute, the Buddha did not conceal the fact but spoke of it as "habitual energy" (*vāsanā*). Why is this? Answer: Although both are distinct delusions...
Because likes and dislikes differ, there is a distinction between concealing characteristics (*saṃvṛta-lakṣaṇa*) and non-concealing characteristics (*asaṃvṛta-lakṣaṇa*).

For instance, when Kāśyapa heard the lute, he was so delighted that he rose and danced; thus, his characteristic was not concealed. When Śāriputra was struck by a flower, he loathed it and deemed it improper, yet despite exhausting his supernatural powers, he could not remove it.
Therefore, the Tathāgata concealed [the matter] by saying, "The habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are not yet exhausted."

The flowers then cling to the body. [Objection: Since the *dharmas as numerous as motes of dust* (*rajas*) do not induce rebirth and do not obstruct the principle, why is it necessary to conceal their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) to clarify that they are identical to the habit-energies (*vāsanā*)?

[Response: Although they do not induce rebirth and do not obstruct the principle, their characteristics must be concealed because these *dharmas as numerous as motes of dust* are distinct afflictions (*paryavasthāna*).

If the Two Vehicles were to know that, in addition to the afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi*) and thought (*citta*), there are further distinct afflictions as numerous as motes of dust, they would become intimidated by the teaching.
Because it would have obstructed the work of conversion at the Deer Park, this was necessarily done by concealing the true appearance. Question:

When Kāśyapa heard the lute and rose to dance in the Vaipulya sūtras, and the great ocean surged with waves while Mount Sumeru rose and fell—did these actually move? If they did not move, the meaning of the text is clear;
if they actually did move, then Mount Sumeru would have entered the water by eighty-four thousand *yojanas* and emerged from it.

"In that case, how could it possibly move? He replied: "Some say it truly moves because all mountains, rivers, the great earth, darkness, form, and space are created by the mind of the eight consciousnesses.
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: 'The mind is like a skilled painter, creating the various five aggregates.
This 'painter' is precisely the mind of ignorance (*avidyā*). However, I fear the meaning of such an explanation is not [correct]."

However, what is now called "non-movement" refers to the fact that when those of the Two Vehicles reach the assembly of the Vaipulya sutras, their *pravṛtti-vijñāna* (active consciousness) has already perished, yet their *karma-vijñāna* (karmic consciousness) still persists before them;
sitting atop the head of ignorance, they perceive movement for themselves. As for what is seen by Bodhisattvas and ordinary beings—the mountains and rivers—are likewise non-moving.
This is, for example, like people of timid constitution who, due to their own mental state, perceive a house as collapsing or turning upside down.

When people see these flowers, they truly do not move; the example remains exactly as it is. Question: Since Śāriputra’s departure from the flowers already involves a distinction, this is precisely a case of seeing [the flowers] as distinct.
Why then is it said that because his residual habits (*vāsanā*) are not yet exhausted, the flowers adhere to his body, and thus he still possesses afflictions of thought (*saṃyojana-kleśa*)?
Answer: Although there are two names, "distinct seeing" and "distinct thinking," their essence is one. When the mind has distinctions, it is called...

Because these are seen separately as the flowers adhere to the body, they are called "afflictions of thought" (*suhuo*). Therefore, the Commentary states: "If one has discrimination regarding the Buddha-dharma, it is not in accordance with the Dharma.
Since there is discrimination, this constitutes "afflictions of view" (*jianhuo*). It further states:

"As long as habitual tendencies (*jixi*) are not yet exhausted, the flowers will adhere to the body; thus there are afflictions of thought. These two names are distinguished for the sake of a general classification; in reality, they are distinct.
Seeing them as distinct, yet contemplating their essence as identical, they are all merely ignorance.

Regarding the "Phrases on the Combined Body and the Honored One with Extraordinary Marks" (*He-shen-zun-te-guang-ming-wen-ju*), this explains the passage concerning the Buddha’s dwelling in the sutras by expanding upon it according to the four teachings, up to the Buddha of the Shared Teaching (*Tongjiao*).
It is then stated that the sixteen-foot body and the *zhunti* (special majestic) body coexist as a unified body within both the conventional and the ultimate truths;

because of this single passage, there have been divergent interpretations throughout the ages. Not only are the applications of the various teachings subtle and profound, but the characteristics of this unified body are also difficult to discern.

Although many predecessors have offered explanations, they all merely derived their understanding by following the literal text. I now wish to resolve these various obstructions by categorizing them into four points and elaborating upon them.

First, the partiality and limitation of the initial teachings; second, the refutation of previous interpretations; third, the correct demonstration of the combined body (*sāmbhogika-kāya*); and fourth, the selection of categories to resolve difficulties.

Regarding the first, the partiality and limitation of the initial teachings: the *Great Master’s Commentary on the Light* (*Guangming shu*) states, "The Buddha of the sixteen-foot body dwells in the Truth (*satya*);

the sixteen-foot body and the *vairocana* (exalted) body dwell together in both Truth and the Middle Way; the *vairocana* body dwells in both the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) and the Middle Way; and the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) [dwells in the ultimate]."

The Buddha abides in the Middle Way. One should first raise a doubt: "If one relies on Tiantai’s Sevenfold Exegesis of the Sūtra, only the *Wenju* (Textual Commentary) on the *Guangming* (Radiance) chapter explains that the 'combined body' (*he-shen*) is the Honored One with Distinct Features (*zuntè*), while it is not clarified within the various other sections [of the sūtras].

Furthermore, among the Four Teachings, why is the meaning of the 'combined body' explained only in the Common Teaching (*tongjiao*), while it is not explained in the other three teachings? One must understand the Great Master’s interpretation.

The transformative applications of the various sūtra schools differ. For instance, the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Sūtra of the Sixteen Contemplations* belong exclusively to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

Although the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* comprises four [teachings], it is not merely the Fourfold Teaching; rather, all four teachings know that the Buddha-nature is eternally abiding. In the first three teachings, there is both provisional application (*shi*) and subsequent abolition (*fei*).

Although the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* also comprises four [teachings], it uses the Great to refute the Small. Furthermore, the *Qing Guanshiyin Pusa Pumenpin Shu* (Commentary on the Universal Gate Chapter of the Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva) explains only the Bodhisattva.

In the *Yuanxing biexing xuanshu*, it is clearly established that although the Great Master’s commentaries on various sutras are all consistent and perfect, the meaning of the "conjoined body" (he-shen) cannot be explicitly clarified therein;

only in this *Guangming* [Sutra] do the four teachings (*sijiao*) discuss it together. Therefore, in his commentary on this section, he clarifies the Buddha’s abiding in principle (*li*) to distinguish the conjoined body.
However, among the four teachings, it is only the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*) that speaks of this, likely because this teaching is vast.
The initial gate primarily penetrates the true reality (bhūtatathatā) while secondarily penetrating the city of transformation;

thus, it penetrates the principle by which the Buddha abides and enables one to abide simultaneously within both the ultimate truth and the provisional manifestation. Therefore, it is necessary to clarify the meaning of the "conjoined body" (saṃbhoga-kāya).
Since this intention regarding the conjoined body is absent in the other three teachings, the doctrine of the conjoined body is not discussed therein.
Next, in refuting the old interpretations, he first poses a question: "Now, the Great Master Tongjiao (Tongjiao Dashi) speaks of the 'combined body' as the six-foot *zhunti* (exalted special) Buddha;
I do not yet know what the characteristics of this combined body are. The first master says: "Regarding the meaning of the combined body in the *Tongjiao* (Shared Teaching):
those who perceive only emptiness see only the six-foot [form]; those who perceive not only emptiness [but also the conventional] behold..."
The Venerable One has specifically noted that because the perceptions of those with dull and sharp faculties differ, it is necessary to clarify the meaning of the "combined body" (*saṃbhoga-kāya*).

[The author] comments: For now, regarding those of dull faculties who perceive only the "emptiness" [of the Buddha], do they merely behold the sixteen-foot form, or do they also behold the "exalted special body" (*vairocana-kāya*)?

If they behold the exalted special body, how can it be said that they "merely behold the sixteen-foot form"? If it is said that they do not behold it, how can it be said that [the two bodies] are "combined"? As for those of sharp faculties, what do they behold?

The meaning of "emptiness" can be understood by analogy with this. The next master says: "If one belongs to the 'combined body' (heishin) of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), they are precisely those who have been grafted onto the Mahāyāna gate;

because they have heard the principle of the Middle Way Dharma-nature, the Tathāgata manifests a superior form upon his inferior response-body, so that by seeking this form, they may attain the Dharma-body.
Thus, the *Fahua shu* states: "[He] wears the appearance of an old bhikṣu."
The manifestation of the *viśiṣṭa-kāya* (the exalted special body) is the characteristic of the Buddha according to the *Tongjiao* (Shared Teaching).

It is further said that if the *viśiṣṭa-buddha* and the *zhàngliù fó* (the six-foot Buddha) both emit light together, this is the meaning of "Shared" (*tong*). What is called "conjoined" (*he*) refers to a single body manifesting two forms simultaneously;

it does not mean that the inferior is identical to the superior. Critique: If one claims that the *viśiṣṭa-kāya* arises upon the inferior body and calls this "conjoined," [it would be a different interpretation].

Furthermore, when [the body] has not yet appeared, one sees only the inferior body and does not see the sublime, special form; when it has appeared and arisen, one sees only the sublime, special form and does not see the inferior body.
Is this not merely seeing them individually? Why is this so? The Three Masters say: "One should know that what is seen as the combined body occurs precisely at the moment of direct encounter.
This is just as in the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), where the eighth stage is hearing the Middle Way and the ninth stage is practicing the Middle Way. Since...

Because those who have not yet realized the Middle Way take refuge in the subsequent teaching, they possess an understanding of the True Truth (*satyadharma*) as realized through that specific teaching;

thus, while perceiving the *janmakāya* (birth-body), they are further able to hear and cultivate the Middle Way. Because they possess an understanding of the *karmavijñāna* (active consciousness), they perceive the *sambhogakāya* (body of honor and excellence).
Since the two understandings of the True and the Middle intersect within their minds, the Buddha-body simultaneously contains both aspects; therefore, it is called "unified" (*saṃhita*).

The critique states: Since one has already heard the central point of instruction, which belongs to those of the Later Teaching (Houjiao), why persist in the interpretation of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao)?

One still perceives the birth-body (shengshen); how much more so when it comes to clearly seeing the marks of the combined body (heyin) and the honored, extraordinary body (zunte xiang)—to speak of them as being identical to a theatrical performance is truly beyond the realm of serious discussion.

Third, regarding the explicit demonstration of the combined body (*sambhogakāya*): one should know that in the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*), there is only the name and meaning of the "combined body," but its specific characteristics cannot be sought.

This is because, in our Patriarch’s *Guanming shu*, while explaining the two characters for the Buddha’s dwelling (*buzhu*) in the sutra according to the four teachings, it is stated that in the Shared Teaching, the Buddha consists of both the *zhangliu* (sixteen-foot) and *zunte* (special majestic) forms combined.
Abiding in the true middle, one thereby attains this teaching; it is thus the initial gateway to the Mahāyāna. This teaching possesses two types of penetration: the proximate and the remote.

It penetrates the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) directly and the city of transformation (*nirmita-nagara*) indirectly; it is primarily for Bodhisattvas and secondarily for those of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*). The remaining six [teachings] belong to the Mahāyāna;

therefore, in this teaching, bodhisattvas of sharp faculties receive the *bié* (distinct) and *yuán* (perfect) stages as a continuation from the *jiē* (intermediate). Within the view of emptiness, they perceive non-emptiness. Thus it is said.
The reason all meanings establish the teaching of the "Dwelling in the True and the Middle" is that it is called the "Combined Body" (Sāmbhogakāya).

Our ancestor Tiantai attained this principle of the "Comprehensive Teaching" (Paryāyābhisamaya-yāna); therefore, one must clearly understand the Combined Body and the Honored Unique Person (Vairocana).

Those who do not comprehend this and yet seek its characteristics are far removed from the truth. It is simply because the purport of the teaching and the intent of the transformation are not understood that erroneous interpretations arise. If one attains this...
The meaning of this is clear.

Regarding the fourfold selection (*catur-vicaya*) that resolves difficulties and answers questions: here, the manifestation of the combined body of the *vairocana* (Universal Radiance) Buddha is specifically explained in reference to the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*), which is the initial gateway to the Mahāyāna.

Because there are bodhisattvas of sharp faculties who receive the transition to the Distinct (*pratyekabuddha*) and Perfect (*vaipulya*) teachings, the combined body of the *vairocana* Buddha is explained. Why is this so? [As for] the text... *(Note: The provided source text ends abruptly with "何故文" [Why is this so? The text...]. The translation reflects the available portion of the passage.)*

The passage clarifies that from the realization of enlightenment of the four Buddhas up to the *Tongjiao* (Shared Teaching), it is said that they manifest the body of a venerable elder bhikṣu while bearing the marks of a *zhunti* (exalted) body.
If this is so, how can a Buddha of the *Tongjiao*, who has merely severed the residual habit-energies (*vāsanā*), be able to manifest such an exalted body? Answer:

Although the distinctions among the four teachings are explained according to their respective degrees of superiority, the body of the eighty-year-old elder bhikṣu in the *Zangjiao* (Tripitaka Teaching) is still taken up within the latter stage of the *Tongjiao*.

Because it is explained according to the meaning of the Separate and Perfect [Teachings], it is said that the manifestation of the "Venerable Extraordinary Body" (zūntè shēn) while bearing the appearance of an old bhikṣu is not something truly existent.

Question: Regarding the General Teaching (Tōngjiào), is the explanation of the Venerable Extraordinary Body based on the four direct teachings (sì zhèngshuō), or is it based on the three transitional teachings (sānjiéshuō)?

If it were based on the four direct teachings, then within that specific teaching, the Middle Way would not be expounded, and the name "Venerable Extraordinary Body" would likewise not exist. If it were based on the three transitional teachings... [four characters missing].

In the ritual manuals (*śāstra-vidhi*), it is clarified that within the beginning and end of this teaching, from the first stage up to the tenth stage, when the conditions of the practitioner’s capacity (*pratibhāna*) ripen, they suddenly sever the remaining habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) through the wisdom of a single thought-moment of correspondence (*ekakṣaṇa-samprayukta-prajñā*).

Seated beneath the seven-jeweled Bodhi tree with celestial robes as their seat, they manifest as a Buddha in an inferior-superior response-body (*hīna-viśiṣṭa-nirmāṇa-kāya*). Answer: Although this passage is based on the four proofs (*catur-upapatti*), here...

Regarding the statement "manifesting an inferior or superior response-body," this is spoken according to the doctrinal principles of the Mahāyāna *Tongjiao* (Shared Teaching), which takes up the meaning of the subsequent [teachings] while incorporating the initial gateway.

Question: The *Wenju* (Textual Commentary) states, "manifesting the body of an old bhikṣu while appearing as a *zhunti* (lofty and special) body," whereas the *Sijiaoyi* (Ritual of the Four Teachings) states, "manifesting an inferior or superior response-body.

How do these two passages differ from or accord with the "combined body" (*he-shen*) *zhunti*? Answer: The text... [The answer continues with a detailed analysis of the distinctions between the various categories of response-bodies.]

Regarding the textual explanations of the Buddha’s attainment of enlightenment through phrases such as these: since there are four distinct teachings with varying degrees of superiority, there are different interpretations.

Some explain that the Buddha appears in a *vairocana-kāya* (special majestic body) while still wearing the robes of an old bhikṣu; others explain him as a combined body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*) accompanied by distinct radiance.

As for the Buddha who abides in principle—the *dharmatā-buddha*—who dwells simultaneously in both [the physical and the principle], this Buddha who can abide within the true [nature] must be explained in terms of the combined body consisting of the six-foot form and the *vairocana-kāya*. Thus, the essential meaning of the texts in both places should be interpreted accordingly.

The arising of different functions differs from existence. Question: Regarding the two types of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*) in which a distinct Buddha dwells—namely, the conventional truth of established convention (*prajñapti-saṃvṛti*) and the conventional truth of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra-saṃvṛti*)—if the conventional truth of birth-and-death is that which is to be subverted, and the conventional truth of establishment is where Bodhisattvas dwell to emerge into the provisional (*upāya*) and transform sentient beings, how is this principle to be understood?
Answer: This refers to the conventional truth in which a distinct Buddha dwells.
This is neither the conventional truth of birth-and-death nor the conventional truth of establishment; rather, it is the conventional truth within the Three Truths.

Because within the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao) there are both the path of teaching and the path of realization—the stage prior to the grounds is conventional, while ascending to the grounds is the Middle—therefore, the Buddha of the Separate Teaching dwells simultaneously in both the conventional and the middle.

Regarding the two types of concentration—on phenomena (*dharma*) and on principle (*tattva*)—the *Sūtra* states that "the Tathāgata dwells in the *dharmatā*," while the *Commentary* says, "He emerges from [this] to narrate the King of Sūtras.

Consequently, there arises the doubt as to whether these refer to concentration on phenomena or on principle, and the objection that there is a contradiction regarding entering and emerging. Now, I shall briefly examine and discuss this by dividing it into four points.

First, the contradiction between the Sūtra and the Commentary; second, the sequence of doubts regarding divergent interpretations; third, the correct judgment of phenomena and principle; fourth, the selection and resolution of difficulties.

Regarding the first, the contradiction between the Sūtra and the Commentary: as for this *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, is it spoken while in meditative absorption, or is it spoken after emerging from absorption?

If it is argued that the statement "the Tathāgata wanders in the Dharma-nature" refers to one who has emerged from meditative absorption (*vyutthita*), while the commentary states that "wandering in the Dharma-nature" describes entering absorption, then how should one judge between these two interpretations?
One should know that this sutra was indeed spoken while [the Buddha] remained in absorption; for within the sutra itself it says: "At that time, the Tathāgata wandered in the Unconditioned..."

Is it not the case that the measurement of the profound *dharmatā* is taught within meditative concentration? If one refers to the *Anantārthasūtra*, it speaks of entering concentration afterward, as it says:

"After the Buddha had spoken this sutra, he entered the *Anantārthasthiti-samādhi*. If one refers to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it speaks of first entering concentration and then preaching the sutra, as it says:
"At that time, the World-Honored One arose calmly from samādhi. Only this light [is mentioned].

This scripture differs from other sūtras in that it is taught entirely while remaining in meditative concentration (*samādhi*). As the commentary states: "The beginning and end of this single sūtra are spoken from within meditative concentration.
Furthermore, at the conclusion of this sūtra, the Bodhi-tree goddess only then requests him to emerge from concentration, saying:
"I pray only that the World-Honored One will manifest his body for me. At that time, the World-Honored One arose from samādhi and praised her, saying: "Excellent, excellent!"
If [the Buddha] were not himself in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), he should not have requested the Buddha to manifest his body at the end of the sutra.
If that were so, why does the Preface Chapter of this newly translated sutra state: "At that time, the Bhagavān arose from samādhi in the late afternoon"?

One must understand that this sutra was spoken while [the Buddha] remained in samādhi; as for the statement in the new translation that he "arose from samādhi," it refers to the conclusion of the discourse.

Appended to the above is the perspective of those with partial capacities regarding the three teachings; as for the perspective of those with complete capacity, from beginning to end they remain within meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Next, regarding those who raise doubts and offer divergent interpretations: how should one distinguish between the matter and the principle of the meditative absorption entered in this sutra?

As for the meditative state of the matter, it must involve both body and mind being utterly tranquil, with eyes closed and pupils withdrawn, remaining perfectly motionless; how could one possibly arise again?

If one maintains that the principle of *li-ding* (the determination of principle) is devoid of the characteristics of coming and going, then from the Buddhas above down to the crawling insects below, there is nothing that is not determined by this principle;
how could such a view be correct? Someone might say: "This sutra is precisely the determination of principle. As it says in the scripture:
