Since both the Sūtra and the Śāstra speak of "contemplating the Buddha," is this not precisely the practice of relying upon the [Buddha’s] environment and its inhabitants (*āśraya-vinaya*)? The *Śāstra* says:

"Taking mental contemplation as the primary principle" means that the three contemplations within a single mind serve as the contemplating subject; therefore, it is called "mental contemplation. This is the traditional interpretation.

People do not understand that the "pointer" is the capacity to contemplate, while the "mind" is the object of contemplation; thus, when subject and object become confused, how can they avoid utter bewilderment?
When first setting out on the path, one must rely upon the sublime realm of Amitābha to practice this contemplation.

When this contemplation is perfected, this Buddha is precisely the Buddha inherent within one's own mind; this mind is the Buddha, and this Buddha is the mind. Thus, the Buddha and the mind are of one essence—this is the contemplation.
Since this is logically tenable, the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) clarifies the Pratyutpanna Samādhi, stating: "That which is called 'Buddha' possesses two meanings:
first, the Buddha seen through the samādhi of one's own mind; second, the Buddha who has realized the fruit through cultivation of causes in the Western Land.

Now, as these two meanings are fully contained within a single object, and in order to accord with the principle, the samādhi is explained according to the former meaning. Once the samādhi is accomplished, it is attained simply by recollecting [the Buddha]."

To see seeing is to take the nature of mind as the Buddha; this is what is meant by "the mind makes the Buddha. According to the intent of this passage, one must first achieve realization through contemplation before one can say, "the mind itself is the Buddha.
It is not that Zhiyi (Sì-míng) lacked this meaning, but rather that he did not distinguish between the initial and subsequent stages.

If one objects, "In the *Xuánwén* [Profound Meaning], why does it say that the phenomena of sentient beings are too vast and the Dharma of the Buddha is too high for a beginner?"—nevertheless, [this remains so].
Regarding the statement that "the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction": it is easier simply to observe one's own mind.
If one claims that observing the Buddha is difficult while observing the mind is easy, one should know that the application of these teachings cannot be treated as a uniform generality.
The *Contemplation Sutra* specifically addresses the two lands of purity and defilement in contrast, intending to cause sentient beings to weary of this Sahā world and seek rebirth in peace.
Relying upon those superior objects as the focal point for contemplation, one abandons the defiled and adopts the pure; it is for this reason that it is so.

The *Miaoxuan* commentary on the sutra was composed to spare practitioners the reproach of "counting others' treasures. Thus, it directs the mind toward internal observation, for contemplating external objects within the distracted realm of the desire world is difficult.
Each [section] follows the meaning of the text, yet the meanings do not follow a single path; let the student examine them deeply.
There is a specific intent here: if one grasps this meaning, one will see for oneself that the previous [interpretations] were incorrect.

The treatment of the obscured mind as being entirely deluded regarding the meaning of the text relies on provisional names to designate the three types of pure karma as the cultivation of the mind.

The essentials of the preface need not be fully elucidated; this is because the sixteen contemplation methods mentioned in the preceding preface were never intended to be exhaustive, being discussed according to the occasion and thus lacking a fixed sequence.
Therefore, the essential doctrine and substance are presented first, followed by the explanation of the title. The *Wǎngshēngjì* states:
"The Great Master did not merely enumerate the doctrine and substance, but also enumerated the title as a single chapter. Hence it says: "The Buddha taught the contemplations."
Regarding the passage beginning with "The *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life*," etc., this is an enumeration of the names;

thus, one knows that the sequence of name, essence (*tattva*), doctrine (*siddhānta*), and so forth is not intended to be inverted, but rather proceeds from the latter back toward the former. However, the meanings explained in these three records are all incorrect.

Now, I shall demonstrate the correct path for you to discern their merits and faults yourself: one should know that the Great Master specifically stated that "mental contemplation" is the doctrine and "true reality" (*bhūtatathatā*) is the essence.
To properly follow the sequence of explaining the meaning of the title, we simply cite the essence and substance of the work.

The title states: *The Sutra on the Meditation on Amitāyus Buddha*. "Meditation" (*guan*) refers to the threefold contemplation within a single mind; as it is the contemplating subject, it is said that the essence of this sutra is "contemplation of the mind.

Amitāyus Buddha’s three bodies in one essence is the object of contemplation; as this is the true reality (*dharmatā*), it is said that the substance of the sutra is "true reality. Thus, these [definitions] accord with the title.

In this "Explanation of the Title," the essence and substance (*tattva*) of the school are specifically highlighted; however, it is only in the subsequent section of the formal commentary on the title that the five meanings are fully elucidated, as the *Shu* (Commentary) states:
"The explanation of the five meanings of the scripture consists of name, essence, substance, function, and the characteristics of the teaching.

If one grasps this intent, the wondrous school is established by the preceding discussion of contemplation, while the subsequent discussion of the title merely clarifies what was not yet expressed in the text. This correction is made because [the previous] discourse was given according to the occasion, and thus [the full meaning] was not present there.

In this sequence, the meaning has no point of return and the text completely loses its spiritual wisdom; the explanations of terms are redundant, the phrasing is deficient, and the characteristics of the teaching are conflated.
If you claim that one should proceed from the end back to the beginning, I now ask: why does this not follow the order of the treatise? Why must it be explained in reverse?

This is because you have failed to investigate the underlying intent, resulting in such erroneous exposition. If one were to examine this through the lens of my current perspective, it would be evident that this concerns not merely the literal meaning of the text.
The brilliance of this [text] likewise causes the essence of the school to be manifest; the essential subtlety of following the title lies precisely here.
If one does not recognize this, there will be no ground upon which to apply the mind. Therefore, I have conducted a thorough investigation and specifically clarified it for you.
If you are still unaware, please consult the original commentary to verify where the meaning truly resides.

Regarding the two types of wholesome deeds—those of meditative concentration and those of distraction—the *Commentary on the Sūtra* states: Question: According to the *Mahāvaipulya*, those who commit the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) or slander the Dharma cannot be reborn [in the Pure Land], yet according to this sūtra, even those with such heinous offenses can be reborn there.

There are two interpretations for this: first, regarding the person committing the offense, there are superior and inferior levels. One of superior faculties is exemplified by King Ajātaśatru, who committed a heinous crime.

There must necessarily be grave remorse that causes the offenses to be diminished and thinned, allowing one to establish roots for rebirth; since those who commit the five rebellious acts (ānantarya) mostly lack such grave remorse, they cannot attain rebirth.
Second, regarding practice, there are both fixed and dispersed modes: the samādhi of contemplating the Buddha is called "fixed" cultivation, while other virtuous deeds are described as "dispersed.
Because the power of dispersed virtue is subtle and weak, it cannot eliminate the five rebellious acts, and thus one cannot go [to the Pure Land].

Since the *Moheben* (Mahāvaipulya) Sūtra speaks of "non-arising" with reference to this very point, whereas this present sūtra clarifies the practice of contemplation and thus speaks of "attaining birth," scholars have traditionally used these passages to distinguish between the two types of wholesome practice:
the settled (*samatha*) and the dispersed (*vikṣipta*). A doubt arises:

if one relies on the *Moheben* Sūtra, where it states that those of the upper and middle grades—residing within or outside the stages of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*)—must cultivate settled wholesome practices and be exhorted to follow the Bodhisattva path, [how does this reconcile with the present teaching?]

That one attains rebirth through the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) also clarifies that this is a practice of meditative goodness (*samādhi-kuśala*). As for the three types of pure karma in the present sutra, these are practices of non-meditative goodness (*vikṣepa-kuśala*).

Why, then, does the Commentary state that the "Great Text" regards non-meditative goodness as not allowing those who commit the five heinous offenses (*pañcānantarya*) to be reborn? This sutra clarifies that through visualization (*bhāvanā*), such persons do attain rebirth.

Furthermore, regarding those of the lowest of the lower grades of rebirth, they are individuals who have committed the five heinous offenses; at the time of death, being oppressed by suffering, they have no leisure to recite the Buddha’s name, yet they encounter [the opportunity].

The teaching of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* (the "Good Spiritual Friend") instructs one to recite the ten recitations (*daśa-namaskāra*) so that the sound does not cease; by completing these ten recitations, one immediately attains rebirth.

How could it be that one must practice meditative contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) before rebirth is attained? Jingjue’s commentary states: "Each of the two sutras [the *Amitābha-sūtra* and the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*] has its own fixed and dispersed practices.

In his sub-commentary, he interprets the passage concerning "contradiction and slander" in the *Larger Sūtra* as referring to dispersed goodness (*saṃbhāra-kuśala*), thereby asserting that the three grades of rebirth in that sutra entirely lack fixed practice (*samādhi*).

Yet it is not known that this is merely a preliminary explanation for interpreting the text; as explained extensively in the *Yibian* (Compilation on Meaning) by Guanzhi, the Great Text universally encompasses all sentient beings of the ten directions who can attain rebirth.

From the tainted ten wholesome acts of the desire realm up to the practices of the Three Sages of the Distinct Teaching, all clarify the wholesome acts of the distracted state (*sāṃkathyadharma*). Furthermore, these are categorized according to the provisional teachings as the cultivation of all remaining wholesome karmas.

If the "scattered good" (dispersed wholesome practices) refers to the sixteen subtle contemplations (*ṣoḍaśa-sūkṣma-vipaśyanā*) of this present sutra, they are specifically intended for those of superior faculties among the audience and belong exclusively to the Perfect Teaching (*ekayāna*).

This constitutes "concentrated good" (*niyata-kuśala*), as detailed in that chapter; although there are ten meanings of its subtlety, they do not go beyond the distinction between the partial and the perfect regarding concentrated and scattered contemplation.
The *Contemplation Sutra* contains only the Perfect and Sudden contemplations, purely clarifying concentrated good, whereas the *Great Sutra* [the Lotus Sutra] is comprehensive.

The distinction between the concentrated (*samāhita*) and the distracted (*vyagra*), and the partial citation of one side, contrasts the textual passages on distracted wholesome deeds with the *Amitāyurdhyāna-sūtra* (Contemplation Sūtra), which exclusively clarifies concentrated practice.
The *Yìyuàn* (Garden of Meaning) states: "Because the *Contemplation Sūtra* clarifies contemplation within the teaching that expresses it, it is called 'concentrated wholesome';

because that [other] sūtra does not clarify contemplation within its expressive teaching, it is called 'distracted wholesome. Such explanations as these do not fully capture the meaning; they all mistakenly recognize the analytical distinctions in reverse order.

The text of this refutation conflates the two scriptures by explaining them through the lens of both the fixed and the dispersed practices; I shall now directly clarify them so that no doubt or obstruction remains.

First, I will present the fixed and dispersed practices of the two scriptures, followed by an exposition on repentance and the re-cultivation of contemplation. Regarding the presentation of the fixed and dispersed practices of the two scriptures:

these two scriptures both encompass the fixed and the dispersed. In those scriptures, they exhort the cultivation of the six pāramitās; among these, the two pāramitās of dhyāna and prajñā—wherein dhyāna is precisely the wholesome state of meditative concentration (samādhi)—constitute the fixed practice.

Wisdom is the cultivation of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). The three types of pure karma elucidated in the present sutra correspond in meaning to "scattered goodness" (*vikṣiptakuśala*). Thus, each of the two sutras has its own specific focus:

scattered and concentrated. The commentary analyzes this by noting that while the other sutra states that those who commit the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*) do not attain rebirth [in the Pure Land] through scattered goodness, this sutra teaches that they can attain it through contemplation.
This distinction is made by contrasting the presence or absence of the cultivation of contemplation regarding individuals who have committed the five heinous crimes as described in these two sutras.

By explaining this, we distinguish between the fixed and the dispersed [karmic conditions]: if the *Mahāvaipulya* states that those who commit the five heinous crimes cannot be reborn [in the Pure Land], this is because it refers to the discourse on dispersed good;

if the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra* states that those with heinous crimes can be reborn, this is because it refers to their cultivation of the meditative good through contemplation, and thus they attain rebirth.

Therefore, one must not use the textual passages concerning the cultivation or non-cultivation of contemplation regarding the five heinous crimes in these two places to create mutual contradictions or obstacles.

Regarding the two sutras on concentration and distraction, those who have never understood that each of the two sutras possesses its own meaning of concentration and distraction, and instead merely explain them by comparing the two against one another, are in error.
Next, concerning the extension of repentance and the renewed practice of contemplation:

although such a person may have committed grave transgressions and be oppressed by suffering at the end of life, if their faculties are sharp and their repentance is profound, then even though the momentary duration is brief, their mental power and vigor will enable them to extinguish their offenses.

Regarding what is called the cultivation of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*): when one encounters a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) who instructs them to practice mindfulness of the Buddha, this is indeed the cultivation of contemplation.

Even though such a person hears the spiritual friend point out that the four elements (*mahābhūta*) are oppressed by suffering and that they should not neglect mindfulness of the Buddha, the spiritual friend further tells them:
"If you are unable to practice mindfulness of the Buddha, you should instead recite the name of Amitāyus Buddha. In this way, with sincere resolve, one should cause the mind to remain uninterrupted.

If one possesses ten recitations, they can dispel distractions; the mind becomes tranquil, wisdom arises, transgressions are extinguished, and enmities are dissolved, leading to rebirth in the Pure Land.

If this is so, then what are the causes and conditions by which those of the lowest of the low grade—who have committed the five heinous crimes and performed the most grievous deeds throughout their lives—encounter a virtuous friend at the moment of death who exhorts them to recite the ten recitations, thereby attaining [rebirth]?

Regarding rebirth in the Pure Land, one should know that although such a person may have committed grave karmic offenses, because they cultivated contemplative practices in the past, they possess seeds of goodness;
thus, at the time of death, they encounter virtuous friends who awaken their latent habitual tendencies. As the *Ten Doubts* (*Shi yi lun*) states:

"Those who encounter a virtuous friend at the hour of death and achieve ten recitations do so because their past karma was strong in goodness, allowing them to meet a virtuous friend for the first time."

The meaning of the text is clear and lucid; why do you not believe it? I shall now provide an interpretation of this passage based on the sutras and commentaries, so that we may together create the conditions for the Pure Land and establish the path to rebirth there.
Part Three: Distinguishing the Objects of Contemplation.

Now, one who wishes to cultivate contemplation must clearly demonstrate the objects and the contemplation; for if these are not recognized, the beginner practitioner has no ground upon which to practice.

Therefore, among the ten objects of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, one first contemplates the aggregates (*skandha*), sense bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*). Since these objects are broad, one discards the elements and sense bases as one would discard a *zhang* to take up a *chi*;
then, one further simplifies from four to consciousness, as one would discard a *chi* to take up an *cun*, contemplating only a single moment of thought.
One who understands the mind is like one who fells a tree by reaching its root, or treats a disease by finding the correct acupuncture point;

however, because the meaning of the text is profound and obscure, divergent interpretations abound. To clarify the great principles, I shall briefly divide the exposition into four parts: first, presenting the text; second, recounting the objections; third, providing the explanation; and fourth, conducting the critical analysis.
First, regarding the presentation of the text: as the *Zhiguan* says, "If one wishes to investigate, one must cut at its root, like cauterizing a disease until the correct point is found.

Now, we shall proceed from the large to the small, from the foot to the inch; setting aside the four aggregates of form and so forth, we observe only the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).

This aggregate of consciousness is precisely the mind. The *Fuxing* commentary states: "Now, 'proceeding downward' means moving from the broad toward the narrow, correctly demonstrating the substance of the object."
The three—aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus)—can all serve as objects of observation. Furthermore, it is asked:

among the five sensory consciousnesses, the mental consciousness (manovijñāna), and the sixth consciousness, which of these consciousnesses and the three types of mind (feeling, etc. that they produce constitute the object of present observation?

Answer: The five sensory consciousnesses and the mental consciousness are certainly the objects of present observation, because they do not yet belong to the afflictions and are of an indeterminate (avyākṛta) nature.
Within the sixth [consciousness], that which grasps what can summon retribution must still be produced; thus it belongs to the realm of afflictions (*kleśa*).

Other types of discrimination belong to the present realm. Furthermore, although these five sensory consciousnesses and the five mental consciousnesses pertain to the present realm, they will be explained in detail below within the section on "traversing conditions and confronting objects."

Second, regarding the presentation of the objection: within the context of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, after eliminating the "zhang" and reducing it to the "chi," and further eliminating the "chi" and reducing it to the "cun," one sets aside the four aggregates of form and so forth and contemplates only the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).

Now, since this consciousness-heart encompasses all three natures (*tri-svabhāva*), does one contemplate all three natures universally, or does one contemplate the indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*) specifically?
If one says that one contemplates the indeterminate nature specifically, yet the aggregate [of consciousness] itself encompasses all three natures...

With what intention do you say that good and evil are not observed? If you claim that they are observed by observing all three natures (*trisvabhāva*), why does the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) state that "they do not yet belong to the afflictions because they reside in the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)"?
How, then, are these two positions to be adjudicated?

Regarding the third point, the explanation: some say that although *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* generally refer to the five aggregates, here one merely sets aside the four aggregates beginning with form and contemplates only the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
Since this does not distinguish between the wholesome and the unwholesome, it is a contemplation that encompasses all three natures (*tri-svabhāva*).

Thus, Zhiyi says: "Because this sixth [contemplation] encompasses the three natures—namely, the wholesome nature, the unwholesome nature, and the indeterminate nature. Others say that although the objective realm of the aggregates generally encompasses the three natures...

The *Śāstra* states that the substance of the object of contemplation is exclusively the neutral (*avyākṛta*), because it excludes both the wholesome and the unwholesome. The *Fuxing* (Supplementary Practice) says: "Because it does not yet belong to the afflictions, it resides in the neutral.

If the *Zhi guan* (Cessation and Contemplation) merely speaks of setting aside the four aggregates such as form and contemplating only the aggregate of consciousness without excluding the wholesome and unwholesome, this is not yet the definitive exclusion;
it is merely like saying one discards the *zhang* for the *chi*, or discards the *chi* for the *cun*, but does not say to discard the *cun*.

Regarding the statement in the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) that "in the sixth [consciousness], one takes that which can summon retribution as the definitive exclusion," and the subsequent point that "in the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*), one excludes the wholesome and unwholesome"—this corresponds to the phrase "removing an inch to reach a foot. These two interpretations are both highly erroneous.

If the first master claims that this refers to a general contemplation of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), why does the *Fuxing* state: "As in the entry into the realm of the aggregates, their essence is non-existent"?

The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states that [the faculty of life] is neither wholesome nor unwholesome, and further says it is "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*) because it does not belong to the afflictions; thus, the meaning of the text is perfectly clear.

Why then must one perversely cling to such a view? Moreover, if the statement regarding the "root and the cavity" were to be rendered in vain, and if the objective sphere of the aggregates (*skandha*) were to encompass both the wholesome and the unwholesome, how could it be distinguished from the sphere of the afflictions mentioned below? How can such groundless talk be worthy of serious evaluation? Next, the Master...
If one were to say that Tiantai had not yet definitively distinguished [the stages] while it was only Jingxi who did so, this too would be erroneous.
Furthermore, within Tiantai’s writings, is there not the meaning of definitively distinguishing even down to the inch and the fraction?

If there is such a distinction yet he does not establish it, it would instead manifest the fault of our Patriarch having failed to exhaust [the teaching], failing to grasp its fundamental source and core intent. If, however, there is no such distinction...
Jingxi established his own system, yet he incurred the fault of contradicting the Patriarchs by adding what was unfounded;

furthermore, if one were to claim that Zhiyi and Guanding had not yet correctly distinguished [the nature of phenomena], then all the great patriarchs from Tiantai onwards who practiced *śamatha-vipaśyanā* would have been observing the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) until they reached Jingxi, who alone then observed the "unrecorded" (*avyākṛta*). This, conversely, reveals that Jingxi surpassed his teachers.

This interpretation does not accord with the original meaning of the text and thus results in this erroneous explanation. My current intention is as follows: if one examines what is presented here, one will see for oneself the error of the previous statement.
One should know that in the correct cultivation of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight), one abandons the "foot" to reach the "inch.

To observe solely the single thought of the cognitive mind (*vijñāna-citta*) is to observe the single thought of the retributive, neutral (*avyākṛta*), unrecorded state; it does not yet involve discussing good or evil. Nevertheless, this single thought of the cognitive mind—
That is to say, the essence of the indeterminate is such that the two minds of good and evil are what arise from it; this should be understood.
First, the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) receives and apprehends the preceding object; next, the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) arises, followed by compliance or resistance.

Subsequently, the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) flows on and performs activity, which constitutes the performance of good or evil. Thus, one knows that the minds performing good or evil all arise from [the indeterminate].

Arising from a single thought-moment of retributive neutral (avyākṛta), one now, within cessation-and-contemplation, moves from the foot to the inch, contemplating only the single thought-moment of the conscious mind.

This means correctly contemplating that the substance of the single thought-moment of the retributive mind is neutral, rather than contemplating the characteristics of the good or evil that arise from it.
If one contemplates the neutral, it is like cauterizing a disease to hit the correct point, or felling a tree by striking its root. Jingxi then says: "It is as follows..."

The substance of the *āyatana* of the aggregates (*skandha*) is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), regardless of whether it is wholesome or unwholesome; furthermore, it is said that because it has not yet been associated with afflictions, it remains in the state of the indeterminate.

According to the intent of this passage, one should specifically contemplate the indeterminate and not the wholesome or unwholesome. This is clearly evident in the Patriarchal texts. How can one stubbornly contradict this?

It is likely because the predecessors did not understand the analogy of the "root and the hole" from the Tiantai school; thus, although they contemplated the single thought-moment of consciousness, [they failed to grasp its true nature].

The substance of the five aggregates (*skandha*) is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), yet their manifest characteristics—whether luminous, wholesome, or unwholesome—are what arise from it. Although one speaks directly of "contemplating the aggregates," this fails to distinguish between the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) and the subject and object, resulting in a confusion between the wholesome and the unwholesome. Now, in the midst of formal cultivation, we select the objects through the three categories: we set aside the *zhang* for the *chi*, and the *chi* for the *cun*. Setting aside the four aggregates of form and so forth, we contemplate only the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*). As it is said: [...the text continues... Regarding the phrase "setting aside the four aggregates of form and so forth": the four aggregates of form, feeling, perception, and formations are all included within the aggregate of consciousness. Therefore, by contemplating the aggregate of consciousness alone, one simultaneously contemplates all five aggregates. This is because the four aggregates are merely the conditions that give rise to the aggregate of consciousness; they do not exist apart from it. Thus, by focusing on the aggregate of consciousness, one naturally encompasses all five. Furthermore, since the four aggregates are the conditions for the arising of consciousness, they are subsumed within the aggregate of consciousness. Consequently, when one observes the aggregate of consciousness, one is already observing all five aggregates. This is why it is said that by setting aside the four aggregates, one contemplates only the aggregate of consciousness. As for the statement "setting aside the *zhang* for the *chi*, and the *chi* for the *cun*": this means that by setting aside the coarse for the subtle, and the subtle for the most subtle, one arrives at the ultimate truth. The aggregate of consciousness is the most subtle of all phenomena; therefore, by setting aside the four aggregates, one contemplates only the aggregate of consciousness. This is the meaning of "setting aside the *zhang* for the *chi*, and the *chi* for the *cun*. As for the statement "it is said": this refers to the teachings of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Setting aside the four aggregates of form and so forth, one contemplates only the aggregate of consciousness.

Since the first four aggregates have already been excluded, excluding the aggregates of perception and mental formations is itself the exclusion of the wholesome and unwholesome minds that arise from them; how much more so when contemplating a single moment of retributive neutral mind?
Furthermore, within the twenty-five expedient methods, to rebuke the five desires and discard the five hindrances is likewise an act of elimination.

Regarding the arising of thoughts of good or evil, when one reaches the stage of "correct cultivation" (*samyak-bhāvanā*), one contemplates only the single thought-moment of consciousness (*vijñāna-citta*);
how could there be room for thoughts of good or evil? It is clear that one contemplates only the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

To make such a statement does not accord with the intent of the textual principles of Tiantai and Jingxi; furthermore, it would cause those practicing *śamatha-vipaśyanā* to confuse the distinction between the object and the contemplation.
Regarding the clarification of the stages of cultivation, examine this meaning carefully; it differs from that of the ancients.
Concerning the fourfold discernment, an ancient asked: "Is it correct to say that the mind-king (*cittarāja*) is the universal substance of both good and evil? Is this interpretation valid?
Answer: This is not yet the case. Jingxi himself stated that the substance of the *āyatana* of form (*rūpāyatana*) is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), and thus neither good nor evil;
how then could he have contradicted this by erroneously judging that the mind-king (*cittarāja*) is the universal substance of both good and evil? Question:

In the three categories for selecting the object of contemplation in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, since one has already excluded the *dhātu*, the *āyatana*, and the four *skandha* of form and so forth, as well as the five sensory consciousnesses and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

Regarding the exclusion [of certain elements] from among the eighteen *dhātus* as stated in the *Sub-commentary* (*Fuxing*), it says: "The five consciousnesses and the fifth mental consciousness are definitely the objects of the present.

Answer: Although they are what is being excluded, this does not mean they are removed. Furthermore, since the five consciousnesses and so forth are all objects of the aggregates (*skandhas*) and are not yet subsumed under afflictions or the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), it is said that they "definitely belong to the objects of the present. Even though they are objects of the present, because these objects are broad and diffuse, at first...
The mind is difficult to construct and must be carefully selected; proceeding from the broad to the narrow, one should demonstrate the essence of the object.

Thus, because the five consciousnesses and so forth are what are to be excluded, observing only the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) is the means by which one attains the faculty and finds the opening—this is precisely the intended meaning. Question:

Since you have already excluded the wholesome and the unwholesome, and are observing only the indeterminate, why does the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) state that "within the sixth [consciousness], one takes that which can summon retribution"?
Furthermore, that which can summon retribution is precisely the "taking" (*grahaṇa*) of good and evil; it does not distinguish between good and evil. Answer:
There is the "taking" in the sense of taking up and using, and there is the "taking" in the sense of selecting and choosing.

Now, when the *Fuxing* says that what can summon retribution is precisely the "taking" of selection, this refers to the act of selecting away the mind that summons retribution; yet one must still be able to give rise to the afflictions belonging to the lower realms.
This does not refer to the "grasping" (upādāna) that constitutes appropriation. Question:

While the five sensory consciousnesses, the five mental consciousnesses, and the sixth consciousness are all capable of producing the three types of mind—feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), and volition (cetanā)—it is possible to speak of the sixth consciousness as having these three minds;

however, how can the five sensory consciousnesses and the five mental consciousnesses be said to possess the characteristic of being able to produce these three minds? Answer: It is simply that they differ in their coarseness and subtlety.

Although these three types of mind—[the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate]—arise in all cases, they differ in their degree of gravity. If the three minds arise for the first time within the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*), they are light and subtle;
the three minds that arise within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) are coarse and heavy.

Furthermore, when the three minds arise in the sixth consciousness with wholesome or unwholesome states manifesting before it, they are even more coarse and heavy than the preceding two. One should know that this applies to the five sensory consciousnesses as well.

The three mental factors of sensation and so forth within the first moment of the five sensory consciousnesses constitute the first instant; the three mental factors of sensation and so forth within that same moment constitute the second instant.
This is the immediate succession of calm abiding and insight.

The various texts that undergo this "reception" (*pratigraha*) encompass a vast range of meanings and intentions; the subtle mysteries of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* clarify both principle and teaching through their mutual examination via the triad of one, three, and one.
While such discourse on reception was easy to understand during the Buddha’s lifetime, it is truly difficult to comprehend regarding the capacity of those to be trained after his parinirvāṇa.

Now, I shall extend its essential meaning, briefly dividing it into four chapters: first, citing the texts; second, demonstrating the difficulty; third, providing the explanation; and fourth, conducting the systematic examination.

Regarding the first cited passage, the "Chapter on the Essential Nature and Characteristics of Śamatha and Vipaśyanā" clarifies that the "distinctive connection" (*bie-jie*) refers to the text concerning the connection to the distinct [teachings]. It asks: "How does one connect via the distinct? The answer is:
First, through the two contemplations of emptiness and the provisional, one exhausts the delusions regarding the ultimate and the conventional truths. Only then does one hear of the Middle Way;

subsequently, one cultivates the contemplation of the Middle to destroy ignorance and manifest Buddhahood through the eight aspects. This Buddha is the fruit, yet it is still based upon the preceding two contemplations.
It is for this reason that it is said the distinct [teachings] connect to the ultimate;

secondly, to demonstrate the difficulty: beneath the Wheel of Dharma of the Buddha’s lifetime, the path was expounded according to the capacity of the audience, clarifying the four proofs and the three connections—this is clearly visible.
Now, the *Mahā-śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Mohe Zhiguan) takes the wondrous section of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* as its lineage to establish the wondrous practice, which is precisely for this purpose.

Why does the practitioner of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching in the Final Age establish this method of contemplation, and why is it further explained through the four proofs? First, regarding "reception" (*jìe*):

what is meant by this? Among the three explanations, some say that because the capacities of sentient beings (*jī*) may be either horizontal or vertical, the modes of reception are accordingly different.

If the capacity is vertical, the practitioner has already heard the *Miaoxuan* and *Wenju*, and having attained understanding and resolution, there is no need to clarify this further within the *Zhiguan*; however, for those whose capacity is horizontal...

Since the mechanism for this has not yet been heard of, and the profound phrases have not been understood to open up the gates of the teachings—failing to discern the characteristics of penetration and obstruction—the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Calming and Contemplation) further clarifies the "single reception.

Someone may say: "The meaning of the 'single reception' in *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* is simply that one uses the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) to receive the provisional truth (*saṃvṛti*), so as to enable the practitioner to harmonize with the characteristics of penetration and obstruction regarding the provisional and ultimate dharmas, thereby exhorting and advancing them toward contemplation of the principle (*tattva-darśana*)."
To shatter ignorance and realize the nature of dharmas or true emptiness, one must first manifest it so as not to remain obstructed by the blockage of emptiness;

only by returning to the penetration of ultimate reality can one truly achieve contemplation of principle. One must clearly understand this single transition. I evaluate these two interpretations and fear that their meanings are incorrect.
The former master follows his own arbitrary whims, erroneously distinguishing between the horizontal and the vertical without any basis. As for the latter master, he claims that...

The "Prior Manifestation of True Emptiness" must clarify the "Single Reception. This serves to suppress the notion that the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature) is distinct [from the other two natures], as it is not a separate principle from the *pariniṣpanna*. Now, to show the correct intent:
one should know that within *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, the "Single Reception" must be clarified.

This is because, within the ten major chapters of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, the first six chapters correctly clarify the opening of understanding (*kai-ge*), while reaching the seventh chapter, "Correct Practice," the ten objects (*daśa-viṣaya*) and the ten [realms] are extensively explained.

My ancestor, the Great Master Zhiyi, contemplated that those practicing *śamatha-vipaśyanā* in the final age might fail to understand within their correct practice that the teachings prior to the *Lotus Sūtra* were expedient means (*upāya*) suited to their respective capacities.
Fearing that such a failure would obstruct the path of contemplation by causing confusion between the provisional and the ultimate,

the Master, following his clarification of the four proofs within the "Chapter on Essence and Characteristics" (where he harmoniously distinguishes between the Truth and Wisdom), further elucidated this point.

Upon first meeting, [the Master] immediately asked: "How does the Distinct Teaching (bie) connect with the Shared Teaching (tong)? The answer was: "First, through the two contemplations of emptiness and provisionality, one exhausts the delusions regarding the ultimate and conventional truths.
Only then does one hear of the Middle Way; yet, one must still cultivate contemplation to destroy ignorance (*avidyā*) and attain Buddhahood through the eight aspects.

This Buddha is the fruit, while the preceding two contemplations serve as the cause; thus it is said that 'the Distinct connects to the Shared. It is for this reason that the Tiantai school [establishes its teachings].
I fear that practitioners, within their contemplation of principle, may become confused regarding the provisional teachings (*upāya*) previously expounded in the sūtras and śāstras;

they may thus encounter obstructions where there should be penetration and consequently harbor doubts, asking: "After the *Lotus Sūtra* opened up the provisional and revealed the real (*satya*), all dharmas are the Buddha-dharma.

The three provisional modes are themselves the ultimate reality, and emptiness and the conventional are themselves the Middle Way. Why is it that in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, [the realization of] the eighth stage..."

Regarding the "cultivation" of the Middle Way within the nine stages and the "realization" of the Middle Way within the tenth stage, one must first destroy the delusions regarding the True and the Conventional before one can hear of the Middle Way.
Is there, then, a Middle Way that exists separately outside of the Empty and the Provisional?

For this reason, our Patriarch feared that practitioners would fail to understand how these sutras and treatises employ provisional means to open up the path of universal reality, only to create obstructions. Therefore, in order to establish the contemplation of principle, he has addressed this in the chapter on "Essential Nature and Characteristics."

In the middle [section], he restates that the teachings prior to the *Lotus Sūtra* already pre-opened the wondrous understanding; one must clarify that this "reception" (*jie*) is not meant to obstruct [the understanding].
Therefore, in the "Discrimination" (*Liaojian*), Jingxi asks: "The *Fahua Xuan* states that 'reception' does not mean 'convergence' (*hui*).

Now, regarding the *Lotus Sūtra*, we should speak only of 'convergence. Why, then, do you speak of 'reception'? The answer is: "Now, in discussing the cultivation of contemplation, it is likewise permissible to restat[e] [this point]."

The teachings prior to the *Lotus Sūtra* are used as examples to discuss the characteristics of openness and obstruction within their respective doctrinal gates; therefore, clarifying them does not hinder the ultimate convergence [of all teachings].
Furthermore, throughout the preceding and succeeding passages, the "conceivable" and so forth are explained everywhere precisely for the purpose of manifesting the "inconceivable";
thus, it is natural that the former should be superseded by the latter in sequence. Why, then, must one ask whether they should not be discussed as being connected?

The intent of attaining this is explained within the section on "Body and Characteristics" (*tixiang*), which describes how the *Lotus Sūtra* was pre-emptively opened through subtle understanding prior to it;
therefore, the treatise connects [the sections] in this manner, and its interpretation of the meaning differs from previous versions.

Regarding the fourfold selection of questions, the *Zhi guan* (Cessation and Contemplation) clarifies the connection, fearing that practitioners of contemplation might not understand the application of provisional means (*shiquan*) in the sūtra sections of transformation.

For this reason, it is explained that there must be a "connection" (*jiejie*). [Objection: If that is so, once one has already completed the opening understanding through hearing the *Miaoxuan Wenju* (The Wondrous and Profound Text and Phrases), why is it necessary to discuss "connection" within the *Zhiguan* (Cessation and Contemplation)?
[Response: Although one has heard the profound phrases and completed the opening understanding, those who practice cessation and contemplation must still further employ the preceding six chapters.
If one does not achieve opening understanding, then upon reaching the stage of formal cultivation, one will fail to comprehend the sūtras and śāstras.

Why does the *Miaoxuan* (Profound Commentary) take the Buddha of wondrous enlightenment as the one who performs the "reception" (*jiejie*), whereas the *Zhi guan* (Stopping and Contemplation) takes a single grade of fruition as the one who performs the reception?

Answer: The *Miaoxuan* correctly clarifies that although there are three types of reception during the Buddha’s lifetime according to the capacities of sentient beings—differing in being Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna—one must discuss their essential indication:
in all cases, it is the Buddha of wondrous enlightenment who acts as the one performing the reception. This applies whether in the *Miaoxuan* or within the *Zhi guan*.

In order to establish the contemplation of principle and prevent confusion regarding the provisional and ultimate truths of the sūtras and śāstras during formal practice, I have preemptively opened up this subtle understanding;

however, since the meaning is already sufficient by connecting the distinct principle to the universal principle, I have therefore clarified only the fruit of a single stage as that which performs the connection.

One who establishes the correct principle of the aggregates (*skandha*) is a model for humanity; a teacher is a raft for the Dharma. If one does not realize that the aggregates are illusory and empty, how can one be fit to serve as a guide for others?
Like being at a crossroads and not knowing which way to turn, one must ensure that afflictions (*kleśa*) do not arise; this requires—
First, one contemplates the realm of the aggregates (*skandha*), because it is precisely those who lack the aggregates who do not incur the burden of receiving a body that manifests before them;

this is why, among the ten realms of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, the aggregates are contemplated first. This is for this very reason. Should there be those who have not yet understood and give rise to heterodox views, they might immediately ask:
"Do practitioners of the Perfect and Sudden (*yuan-dun*) path who cultivate *śamatha-vipaśyanā* still establish the aggregates? If you say they do establish the aggregates..."

The *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the *Fahua wenju*) states that the ten objects of contemplation, such as the aggregates (*skandhas*), exist only within the Three Teachings. If one were to argue that [the Ten Objects] are not established [in the Perfect Teaching], this is not so;

for in the "Chapter on the Correct Practice of Stopping and Contemplation" (*Zhiguan zhengxing zhang*), the ten objects are fully elucidated, beginning with the contemplation of the aggregates (*skandhas*). Since the heavy burden of the five aggregates is constantly manifest before us, is this not the establishment of the aggregates?
To those who offer a response, some say: "The Perfect [Teaching] takes non-partiality as its meaning and absolute transcendence (*juedai*) as its function, from beginning to end."

The nine realms of non-duality are themselves the Buddha-realm; there is no need to establish the objective spheres (*viṣaya*) of the aggregates (*skandha*). As the *Shiǎn* (Commentary on the *Zhiguan*) says:

"The ten objective spheres, such as the aggregates, exist only within the Three Teachings. The critique states: If one does not establish the aggregates, then the objective sphere of the aggregates in *zhiguan* (calm abiding and insight) becomes redundant.

Furthermore, for which teaching are the objective spheres of the aggregates, sense bases (*āyatana*), and so forth intended? If they are intended for those of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), why not establish the aggregates? If they are intended for those of the partial capacity (*pianji*), [then they belong only to the Three Teachings].

It can be known that the intention behind [the claim that] it is neither *śamatha* nor *vipaśyanā* is erroneous. Some say: "If one demonstrates the limits of the object and the contemplation (*ālambana-vipaśyanā*), then there are the *skandhas*;

if one enters through the practice (*bhāvanā-praveśa*), then there are no *skandhas*. This is because the ten objects of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* merely demonstrate the characteristics of the practitioner’s object and contemplation;

when one initiates the cultivation, one realizes that the *skandhas* are none other than the wondrous. As the *Fuxing* (Supplementary Practice) says: "The form and mind from beginningless time are fundamentally wondrous."
The objects of the realms are wondrous, yet wisdom follows along with their deluded transformations; one neither perceives nor knows this.

Now that you have heard their names, you know that the *skandhas* (aggregates) are precisely these four aggregates and that the mind is the eternally abiding, wondrous principle. [Commentary: Since both the objects and the contemplation are shown, there must be both the subject who contemplates and the object contemplated.
How could it be that only the objects are shown while no one is shown to practice the contemplation? Otherwise, the objects shown would become a mere empty establishment.

Those who do not understand the contemplation of objects merely speak from their own arbitrary conceptions; since there are many divergent interpretations, I shall not record them here. What I am now showing differs fundamentally from what preceded.

One should know that within the Perfect and Sudden Teaching (*yuantun jiao*), if the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth are not established as objects, where would the wondrous contemplation be applied, and where would the wondrous object be manifested?
If one is separated from the three paths (*trividhamārga*), there are no three virtues (*triguṇa*); it is just like [the absence of] afflictions [if there were no path].

Affliction is itself bodhi; birth-and-death is itself nirvana. Regarding the ten vehicles of cessation and contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) and the three contemplations, first one contemplates the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth.

Just as one discards the *zhang* to take up the *chi*, and discards the *chi* to take up the *cun*, one contemplates only the single thought-moment of consciousness. Is this not establishing the aggregates?

If the aggregates were not established, what would serve as the object of contemplation? What would serve as that which is to be realized? And what would serve as that which is to be revealed in its perfection?
The practitioner of sudden practice contemplates the wondrous realm through wondrous contemplation, realizing that the aggregates (skandhas) constitute the inconceivable;

they understand that the very substance of these phenomena is, in its suchness, the three thousand realms within a single thought-moment. As it is said, "the substance of the hindrances is itself virtue," there is no need for them to be transformed or eliminated.

If there were no aggregates, what would there be to transform? This differs from the Separate Teaching (biejiao), which indirectly negates the provisional and directly points to pure *tathatā* as the object of realization.

What distinguishes this [from other interpretations]? If that were so, and since you have established the aggregates (*skandha*) as the objective realm (*viṣaya*), why does the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary) state that "the ten realms, such as the aggregates, exist only within the Three Teachings"?

This is because the substance of the aggregate-realm is precisely what the practitioners of the Nine Realms within the Three Teachings—the three paths, three obstructions, four maras, four eyes, and two wisdoms—take as their object of contemplation. If it were not so, the *Shiqian* would not have used the term "aggregates."
The ten objects [of contemplation] exist only within the three vehicles; these are now the objects of observation for those of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*).
The text states "only the three vehicles" because this is explained according to the specific nature of the ten objects as they pertain to the three vehicles.

Since it is said that these are the objects of observation for those of the Perfect Teaching, the meaning of establishing the [five] aggregates (*skandha*) is already revealed therein. If this is so, why is the Buddha-object not established among the ten objects?

The intention is as follows: the nine objects below are explained in relation to past habitual tendencies. Because one observes the present aggregates (*skandha*) by waiting for them to manifest, they are observed only now.

Regarding the Buddhas of the three previous vehicles, there are teachings within the cause but no person in the fruit; since there was no cultivation in the past, these [nine objects] are not established for them now.

Regarding the *Kula-kula* (House-to-House) classification in the verses of the Tripiṭaka of the Hīnayāna, after the attainment of the first fruit (*srotāpatti*), there are differences in the progressive severance of the afflictions of desire; thus, the *kula-kula* spiritual capacity arises.

As for those that are particularly difficult to adjudicate, they are found solely within the verses of the *Abhidharmakośa*; regarding these, the literary expositions of those who have lectured on them throughout the past and present are [various].

This work has circulated widely in the world, and while I have examined various commentaries and found this one superior, I now further assist its completion so that it may be bequeathed to future generations.

A brief evaluation of its essentials is divided into four chapters: first, presenting the doubts; second, critiquing previous interpretations; third, assisting the correct view; and fourth, addressing remaining obstacles.

First, regarding the demonstration of those with doubt: the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states: "Having abandoned three or four categories [of afflictions], one is a 'family-to-family' (*kulaṃkula*) who has two or three births remaining.

Having abandoned five, one is a candidate for the second fruit; having abandoned six, one is a once-returner. Regarding this verse, does it describe sequential abandonment (*anupūrvakṣaya*) or leap-over abandonment (*vyutkrāntaka*)?

If it describes sequential abandonment, then for one who abandons two [categories], there must necessarily be three; and for one who abandons five, there must necessarily be six. This is the meaning of the present verse.

Regarding the statement that one may abandon up to the third or fourth [grade of defilement], if it is argued that the verse speaks of "leaping over" (ultra-passing) both calm abiding and insight, why does it say "if one leaps over"?

Furthermore, while abandoning up to the fifth grade is called "one who goes from family to family" (kulaṃkula), it does not mention leaping over the third or fourth grades. How, then, are these two alternative paths—leaping over versus sequential progression—to be categorized and subsumed?
Second, regarding the evaluation of the ancient masters who mutually taught one another, they say that there are three types of severing the nine grades of afflictions of desire:

first, sequential severance (*anupūrva-prahāṇa*); second, skipping-severance (*vyutkrāntaka-prahāṇa*); and third, transcendent severance (*atikrāntaka-prahāṇa*). In the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā*, it does not mention sequential severance; rather, it mentions skipping-severance and, in the verses themselves, transcendent severance.

The *Fuxing* (Supplementary Practice) commentary states: "One who initiates great preparatory effort is a 'transcender' (*atikrāntaka*) because, while previously in the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), they have attained [the path] within the realm of desire."

When one reaches the sixteenth moment of mind, by adding untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) to the meditative concentration of the desire realm and initiating the practice of diligence (*vīrya-pratipatti*), one is able to sever the afflictions;

therefore, it is called "preparatory application" (*prayoga*). It is not that after seeing the truths (*satyadarśana*), one further cultivates the untainted path and names that "preparatory application. The critique states:

The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* says that it is the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) who proceeds to sever the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*); furthermore, it says that the proceeding to sever them is spoken of after the fruit of stream-entry.
If "transcendental severance" (chao-duan) refers to this, it should mean that one severs the afflictions of cultivation (si-huo) by means of the sixteen moments of mind prior to the first fruit;
only then could it be called transcendental severance. If that is so, why does the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) state: "Because the noble ones (ārya) initiate great preparatory effort"?
Since it specifies "noble ones," this must refer to the period after the first fruit; how then can it say they apply untainted practice (*anāsrava-caryā*) upon the sixteen moments of mind?

Furthermore, regarding the statement in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* that "if one transcends [the first] abandonment up to the fifth stage, it is called 'family-to-family' (*kulaṃkula*)," the verse-text itself states that one abandons three or four grades of afflictions;
how then could this be a case of "transcending" (i.e., skipping) the abandonment? There are many further errors, which I shall briefly indicate.

Master Chou judged that the verse-text of the *Abhidharmakośa* correctly describes the subsequent abandonment, yet after establishing this certainty, he himself again raised a doubt, saying: "If the verse-text refers to the subsequent abandonment..."

Jingxi asks: "If there is both 'leaping over' (*cāra*) and 'sequential' (*anupūrva*) progress in advancing to sever the third and fourth [categories of afflictions], and since it says 'if leaping over,' should one not also include a verse on leaping over in the severance?
He himself explains: "This text is precisely within the discussion of the sequential method;

it discusses the practitioner who, while intending only to sever three categories, has the power of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) such that it invades and severs the upper category of the middle [set]. This is illustrated by the metaphor of splitting bamboo: while intending to break through three nodes, the blade [severs more]."
The sharp edge of the critique penetrates as far as the fourth section; this case is likewise so. The evaluation states:

If this master claims that the verse text follows the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* in its sequential order and thus cites the *Fuxingji* (Supplementary Record) as proof—whether it be sequential or non-sequential—then this is a mistaken judgment regarding the text of the *Fuxingji*.

This passage by Jingxi was written precisely because the Great Master, in his *Zhi guan*, was about to skip over [the stages] and designate the "five grades" (*wupin*) as the stage of severance (*duan*).

Master Jingxi then took the verses and sequentially divided them to correlate them with the *Śrāvakabhūmi* (Zhiguan), discussing both the "small leap" (*xiao chao*) and the "house-to-house" (*jia-jia*) stages together.
He then concluded by stating, "Whether by leaping over or proceeding in sequence, advancing to sever the third or fourth [fetters] is precisely the summary.

This conflates the *Abhidharmakośa* with the "small leap. How could these verses from the *Abhidharmakośa* ever have been intended solely to clarify that [specific] doctrine? Such an error is improper.
Take this up.
Third, as for those who assist what is correct: if it is appropriate according to principle, why must one seek others to assist in praising what has been clarified?

Since the profound marks and meanings are already in accord with the tracks [of the truth], how could they not be followed and practiced? As the *Fuzan* says: "Since the treatise states that one is already a stream-enterer..."

Regarding the progression toward abandoning the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), if three conditions are met, one is termed a *kulaṃkula* (one who goes from family to family).

Furthermore, it is said that after the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna-phala*), one speaks of progressing to abandon the afflictions; if these were not abandoned in successive order, how could it be said that one speaks of progressing to abandon the afflictions after the fruit of stream-entry?

Thus, we know that there is no room for doubt regarding the person who abandons [afflictions] in succession according to the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā*. Moreover, the *Zhiguan* states: "One abandons a single grade of desire-affliction in succession."

Up to the fifth grade [of defilements], all are termed candidates for the stage of Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*). If one transcends and abandons [the defilements] up to the fifth grade, they are termed "Family-to-family" (*kulamkula*).
Subsequently, the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) proceeds to correlate the sequence of abandonment from the *Abhidharmakośa* with that of the *Śikṣānanda* and *Zhiguan*.

It then states that the person who "smallly transcends" is immediately correlated [with this], saying: "The meaning of this sequential abandonment is the same as that in the present text. Thus, it is known that both sequential abandonment and small transcendence are...

Having thus established the meaning of the *kulaṃkula* (one who goes from family to family), he concludes by summarizing: "Whether by skipping or by proceeding in order, one abandons three or four [defilements].
If this is so, how should one reconcile the case of the person who proceeds in order—who abandons three or four themselves—with the "small-leaper" (*alpātikrānta*), who leaps over five categories?

It should be understood that although the small-leaper abandons five categories, because the fifth category and the sixth category share a single common moisture (*sneha*), [the leap is considered equivalent].
Having grasped this meaning while at Jingxi, Zhiyi subsequently judged that these five stages (pañca-vastūni) are identical to the four stages;

thus they may be harmonized with the sequence of the doctrine of "successive abandonment" (*krama-prahāṇa*). Since this aligns with the present text, we know that the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* itself teaches successive abandonment.
When Zhiyi states, "Because the Noble Ones initiate great preparatory effort (*prayoga*)," does this not clarify that the verses of the *Kośa* anticipate [this doctrine]?
Does one sever the afflictions by means of a subsequent deliberation upon the Truth, augmented by untainted practice, following the fruition of the flow?

Regarding this teaching, there are three points to be gained: first, it correctly adjudicates the verse of the *Abhidharmakośa* concerning the person who severs afflictions through subsequent [deliberation];

second, it elegantly accords with the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), harmonizing the intent of the *Abhidharmakośa*, the *Śrāvakabhūmi*, and the *Mohe Zhiguan*; and third, it profoundly investigates the two types of faculties: those that transcend the sequence and those that follow it.
Regarding the nature of these [attainments], all treatises state that there are these three types of *kulaṃkula* (one who goes from family to family); one must certainly grasp this.

Fourth, regarding other obstructive questions: the *Śrāvaka-vibhāṣā* (Old Vibhāṣā) explains that those who have "slightly transcended" attain the status of *kulaṃkula*, whereas those who have "fundamentally transcended" do not.
If this is so, both of these two types of persons have previously, while on the stage of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*), suppressed the afflictions of the realm of thought (*bhavāgra*).
Regarding the question: "From the point where the quantity of delusions is reduced down to the sixteenth thought-moment, one transcends all afflictions of the realm of form (dhyāna-delusions).
Why is it that while the 'Lesser Transcender' (kṣudra-saṃkrāntin) is discussed, the 'Family-to-Family' (kulaṃkula) stage is not discussed for the person who has already transcended? Answer:

When the person who has already transcended was at the level of an ordinary being (pṛthagjana), although they had suppressed the afflictions of the realm of form, because their power of wisdom based on the out-flowing (sāsrava) dharmas was weak, they are not discussed as being in the "Family-to-Family" stage. As the *Fǔxíng yù* states: "Although..."

If one has severed five grades [of afflictions], they are merely called a candidate for the first fruit; if one has severed all six grades, they are simply said to be a candidate for the second fruit.
By analogy with this principle, it is clear that the status of a "family-to-family" practitioner (*kulaṃkula*) is not considered here. Question:

If there is no case where one dies after having exhausted the great grades of afflictions without severing them, why is it that when one has severed eight grades but not yet reached the ninth, one does not attain the fruit? Jingxi answers himself: First, because it obstructs the fruit.

Second, regarding those who transcend the realms (*dhātu-vyatikrānta*), we now pose this question: Is there anyone who abandons from the eighth to the ninth [grade of affliction]? If you say there is, then Master Jingxi should not have posed this question. If you say there is not, then among those who abandon progressively (*anupūrva-prahāṇa*), could there not be those who abandon from the eighth to the ninth? Answer: What kind of statement is this? In the three cycles of the *Lotus Sūtra*, all are cases of progressive abandonment; even the root-natured (*indriya*) practitioners [proceed] in this manner. Furthermore, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states: "The Bodhisattvas of the first stage abandon the afflictions of the desire realm up to the ninth grade. Why does the *Miaoxuan* state that after the mind of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), one must further cultivate the sixteen aspects?

Question: For a person who "leaps over" (the intermediate state), do the three conditions for attaining the status of a *kulaṅkula* (one who goes from family to family) still apply? If one were to say...

If the conditions are complete, there are only the first and last two conditions; if they are incomplete, the treatise states: "If three conditions are complete, it is termed 'Family-to-Family' (kulaṃkula) or 'Small Leaper' (svalpātikrānta).

Since there is no antidote for those [who lack the conditions], and thus no untainted faculty (anāsrava-indriya), how can one also clarify the case of the Family-to-Family practitioner when there is only the single condition of contemplating reality?
Answer: The predecessors have explained this in detail, stating that one must clarify the second untainted faculty.

One-pointed concentration on the present is not like this; one must know that the treatise speaks specifically of those who abandon [the defilements] in successive order, as there is no such thing as "minor leaping-over" (kṣudra-vyatikrama) here, and thus it need not be explained.
This is because former scholars did not understand the intent of the Abhidharmakośa school nor the faculties and dispositions of the Sautrāntika tradition, leading to these erroneous explanations.

The *Chetisengyi* (The Correct Meaning of the Vehicle Body) clarifies that the "vehicle body" (*chenti*) and the "mounted body" (*shengtai*) differ only as a metaphor for the Dharma; their underlying principle is one and the same.

This is because both "vehicle" (*che*) and "mounted" (*sheng*) take "movement" (*yundong*) as their essential meaning, as the *Zhuan* (Commentary) states: "Movement is the meaning of carrying. The *Yi* (Book of Changes) says: "The sun... [and so forth].
The movement of the moon is called "transportation" (*yun*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "transporting on land is called *yun*.

What is referred to as "riding" (*cheng*) is the harmonious integration of the three tracks, which is termed the "Great Vehicle" (*Mahāyāna*). Because one rides upon this vehicle and is able to transport sentient beings so they may emerge from the suffering of birth and death, it is called a "carriage.

As for the "three tracks," these are precisely the true nature (*tathatā*), contemplative illumination (*vipaśyanā*), and supportive accomplishment (*sambhāra*). Furthermore, these three tracks pervade all...

Regarding the four teachings, the Tripitaka and Distinct (Vaipulya) teachings take contemplative illumination as the essence of the vehicle, while the Shared and Perfect teachings take true nature as the essence of the vehicle.

Now, concerning the Tripitaka and Distinct teachings, taking contemplative illumination as the essence of the vehicle is easy from the perspective of the Dharma, but difficult from the perspective of analogy.

Why is it easy from the perspective of the Dharma? Because contemplative illumination is itself contemplative wisdom; its function is to destroy delusions and serve as a support for the accomplishment of merit.
Regarding the "verification of the true nature" (zhenxing) by Master Dezhuang, this is manifested upon the fruition and is thus visible.

As for those who raise objections based on analogies—since they take contemplative illumination (*guanzhao*) as the essence of the vehicle—it remains unclear what they intend to designate as its precursor.

One should know that the two teachings of the *Āgama* (Zangjiao) and the *Vaipulya* (Biejiao) are teachings concerning the non-identity between the internal and external realms; therefore, they take contemplative illumination as the essence of the vehicle. Since this is so...

One does not point directly to the fruit as being present [at this moment], because it is only upon proceeding from cause to fruit that the true nature (*dharmatā*) is revealed; therefore, contemplative illumination (*vipaśyanā*) is taken as the essence of the vehicle (*yāna*).
As the *Shu-ji* (Commentary) states: "In both the *Āgama* and *Vaipulya* teachings, wisdom is universally taken as the essence.

If the true nature of these two teachings were only perfected when the fruit is fulfilled, then if one were to point to the essence as being present [in the future], by what means would one proceed? If one employs contemplation..."
If one illuminates [the path], then from beginning to end, one knows through this that the distinctiveness of the "Treasury" (the *garbha*) lies in whether it is within or outside the realms;
since both the provisional and the direct teachings are not identical [to the ultimate], they take contemplative illumination (*vipaśyanā*) as the essence of the vehicle (*yāna*).

As for the two teachings of the Shared and the Perfect, they take the true nature track (*tathatā-gati*) as the essence of their vehicle, with contemplative illumination serving as the precursor and the completion of practice acting as its adornment. This is easy to understand by way of analogy, though difficult to grasp by way of the Dharma itself.
Colophon to the *Collection of the Elite of the Tiantai School*:
The study of the Tiantai and Tiantong traditions reached its zenith in the Venerable Zhili of Ming; he revived and exalted it with brilliance and grandeur—how magnificent was his achievement!
Not only did he refute the heterodoxies of successive generations, but he was also able to guard against the perilous paths of future ages. Therefore...
There were those, such as Bei Zong of Xiachuan, Po Zu of Shenzhi, and Xie Yijian of Zhuanan, who held divergent views;
upon seeing the clarity of the purple and vermilion [of this work], scholars no longer wept at the crossroads.

Only Master Puming of Xiandu possessed exceptionally outstanding insight and was endowed with abundant talent; though he relied on the teachings of Siming, he did not accept them entirely, and thus composed [this treatise].
A collection of several scrolls of doctrinal teachings entitled *The Essence of the Tiantai School* (Rùn) was recently obtained by me at Chōryū-ji in Nō;
upon reading it once, I remarked that the Master’s learning and insight transcend his peers and his arguments are profound.

While he certainly relied much upon Siming for his supplementary expositions, the independent views he established are sufficient to stimulate the correct doctrine—truly what is called "the other mountain."
This stone is for grinding jade.

Last year, in the year Jia-wu, our Wheel-Turning King (the Great King) first presided over the affairs of the Tiantai school throughout the world; he was diligent in the study of the Way and personally initiated [its propagation], being especially refined in the discourse of the Four Ming masters.
He once presented this book and commanded its rapid circulation, whereupon it was entrusted to the printing blocks by Shengyi.
The scholars of our academy lament that the first fascicle is missing and that from the sixth fascicle onwards has also been lost;
it is my hope that future gentlemen will obtain a complete copy to supplement and restore this work.
Written respectfully by the śramaṇa Ryōjun of Tōei Jōshō-ji,
on a winter day in the year of Yiwu (1575), the fifth year of the Zhengde era.
